maintopic: SECRETARY OF STATE-REPLY TO QUESTIONS ASKED ON ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other evening when my estimates were under discussion, I undertook with the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to reply to certain questions about the civil service commission about which I did not have information available at that time. I think the easiest way for me to reply, if you will permit me to do so, Mr. Speaker, is to read a letter I have received from the chairman of the civil service commission. It replies to both questions and I think that it contains practically all the information on the subject that can be put succinctly. The letter reads as follows:
June 17, 1954.
Dear Mr. Pickersgill,
With reference to the questions of Mr. Michener and Mr. Knowles last evening as to the number of "civil servants, in round figures, for whose appointment the civil service commission is responsible, and the total payroll of that group of civil servants", as well as "the balance of the payroll", and also "the number of permanent and temporary civil servants", the latest available information as contained in a memorandum of the dominion bureau of statistics for the month of February, 1954, shows that in the "classified" positions of the service, which are almost entirely composed of the appointments under the jurisdiction of the civil service commission, there were 135,884 employees with a payroll for the month of $34,819,104. Of these 76,938 were temporary and 58,946 were permanent employees. The comparative figure for 1949 was 123,924, of whom 86,015 were temporary and 37,909 were permanent.
In the remaining section of the service there were 22,245 prevailing rate employees, 10,861 casuals and 1,770 ships' crews, with a payroll for the month of February, 1954, of $6,850,943.
Yours faithfully,
C. H. Bland,
Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, when the
committee last considered this item of the estimates on April 30 numerous members joined in expressing their pleasure at the fact that the Minister of Agriculture was restored to health and was back in the house. I should like to join those members in expressing my pleasure that the minister continues in good health and I hope he will for many long years. In his speech on April 30 the minister quoted quite a number of statistics regarding cash income from the sale of farm products for the last ten years. From these figures one would be led to believe that the agricultural industry in this country is quite prosperous, and the impression was left that it was not only prosperous in a general way but prosperous all over the country in every particular.
When I visited my riding not long ago I happened to meet a neighbour of mine who is a farmer. He went to town with me and on the way he said: "I am going to town because I have sold some of my cattle in
[Mr. Langlois (Gaspe).l
order to meet the next payment on my farm improvement loan for my tractor." I asked him how it came about that he was selling cattle to meet this obligation, and he said that it had been a tough year. I said to him: "That cannot be so. The Minister of Agriculture says it is a very prosperous year and he has statistics to prove that you never had it so good." The reaction of my friend was rather astonishing or surprising. He was moved to quote Disraeli. I do not know whether he was conscious of quoting Disraeli but he said: "There are three kinds of lies; there are lies, damned lies and statistics."
That made me realize the importance of examining very carefully statistics which are put forward to support any argument. In the light of whatever knowledge I happen to have regarding statistics I thought it wise for me to examine the figures which had been given by the minister. I also thought it wise to try to increase my knowledge of statistics and the traps into which the unwary may fall if they try to follow statistics without examining very closely what they really mean. I remembered H. G. Wells' comment on our modern civilization when he said that statistics will one day be as necessary for efficient citizenship as the ability to read and write.
With the large volume of statistics that is being thrown at us by government bureaux and other organizations in recent years, I think that time has already arrived. After all, we must have very sceptical minds in order to deal intelligently with such things as advertisements for tooth paste, travel circulars, claims for patent medicines and some statements which are made by chronically optimistic cabinet ministers.
Therefore in self-defence I felt it was wise for me to try to learn a little more about statistics. In line with that idea I got a book which might help me to interpret statistics a little more accurately. I should like to quote from the introduction to the book. In one place it says:
The secret language of statistics, so appealing in a fact-minded culture, is employed to sensationalize, inflate, confuse and oversimplify. Statistical methods and statistical terms are necessary when reporting the mass data of social and economic trends, business conditions, "opinion" polls, the census. But without writers who use the words with honesty and understanding and readers who know what they mean, the result can only be semantic nonsense.
The author goes on to say:
This book is a sort of primer in ways to use statistics to deceive. It may seem altogether too much like a manual for swindlers. Perhaps I can justify it in the manner of the retired burglar whose published reminiscences amounted to a graduate course in how to pick a lock and muffle

a football:	The crooks already know these tricks;
honest men must learn them in self-defence.
It is in self-defence that I have resorted to this book. Incidentally, the title of it is "How to Lie with Statistics". I do not mean to imply that dishonesty has been used by any cabinet minister. I think statistics are legitimate material for supporting an argument, but nevertheless by that very fact it becomes necessary for those who are required to present and support the other side of the argument to try to interpret these statistics intelligently. I should like to refer briefly to the speech that the minister made on April 30. It appears on page 4280 of Hansard and reads in part as follows:
I have in my hand a summary table, "cash income from the sale of farm products and from supplementary payments over the years, from 1942 down to the present". I have had those years following
1942	divided into three-year periods; my reason being that we have considered, in arriving at conclusions, that it is not advisable just to take one year and compare it with other years before or after.
It is much better to take three-year periods and compare one three-year period with a like three-year period. From 1943 to 1945 we had income from farm products in the east amounting to $655 million the first year, $703 million the second year and $770 million the third year, or a total of $2,128,562,000. Following the same plan, in the next three-year period we had in the east $2,871,173,000. But I think it probably would be better if I were to take east and west side by side rather than to go through one list and then the other. Therefore going back to the first three-year period, income from farm products amounted to $2,128,562,000 in the east and $2,858,770,000 in the west. In the next three-year period the figures are $2,871,173,000 in the east and $3,348,716,000 in the west. In the third period, from 1949 to 1951, the figures are $3,605,406,000 in the east and $3,952,669,000 in the west. So far as the last period is concerned, we have only gone through two years of it and the figures are $2,444,668,000 in the east and $3,129,903,000 in the west.
I have made an estimate of what the amount is likely to be over the three-year period, and at this time I will read the total amounts for all Canada in each of the three-year periods. They are: from
1943 to 1945, $4,987,332,000; from 1946 to 1948, $6,219,889,000: from 1949 to 1951, $7,558,075,000; and for the last period of two years $5,574,571,000. If I were to add to the last figure the estimate for the present year that total would be $8,200 million worth in each for farm products.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in examining those figures we must realize that, in the first place, in each case we are given two different bundles of figures; one for all of western Canada and the other for all of eastern Canada. Those figures are quite accurate:	I do
not reflect on them in any way. But it must be realized that they do not express in any way agricultural conditions in certain smaller areas which are bundled in with an area that may be prosperous. There is no reference to each year. There again, we have the statistics in a bundle and we have the figures
Supply-Agriculture
for three years together. We may have a very bad year that will put a lot of farmers into bankruptcy, but when you lump that one year in with two other years that have been relatively good the result looks acceptable.
You will notice also, Mr. Chairman, that these figures are for cash income. There is not necessarily any relationship between a farmer's cash income and his profits for a year. There is no indication, either, of the number of farmers amongst whom this amount of money was divided. The minister gave no figures, and I have none, to indicate the number of farm operators who had to share this total cash income. There is no indication of the number of people who were fed from the products of the farmers who received this cash income. Our population is going up very rapidly. Canadian farmers are feeding 15 million people in Canada this year, at least to a great extent. Our food is not all produced in Canada, of course, but the major portion of it is. A number of years ago the population was much smaller, so the amount of food produced for the cash received has gone up and therefore the cash receipts should naturally go up in proportion for the individual farmer to be as well off.
Then, another thing of which we should take note is that so far as the figures for 1954 are concerned the minister made an estimate. He extrapolated two figures for last year and the year before and said they are probably such and so for the present year, and arrived at a figure for the three years in order to convince the farmers that they are prosperous. It may be possible to do that in some areas, but I am afraid the minister will not succeed in the area from which I come. In this area the small operator is in a continually worsening position. The big specialists who produce milk for cities and operate on a large scale near the city are getting a bigger and bigger slice of the cash income for farm products.
What I am chiefly concerned with, of course, is agricultural conditions in my own province of Prince Edward Island. I should like to put some figures in that regard on the record. The first thing I want to indicate is the cash income for 1951, 1952 and 1953. The figures in all cases are for three years. Incidentally, these were the figures the minister gave for all Canada. The figures for Prince Edward Island are as follows: for 1951, $26 million; for 1952, $31 million; and for 1953, it was down to $22 million, a drop of about 30 per cent in one year.

Where did you get those statistics?

Supply-Agriculture

I got them from the dominion bureau of statistics report on farm net income for 1953.
The net income for those three years is $17 million, $20 million and $12 million, that is a drop of 40 per cent in one year in the net income. After all, that is what the farmers' profits are.
Now, on the other side of the ledger, let us examine what has been happening to the farmers' operating costs. This applies to Prince Edward Island. We will start out with taxes. In 1951 the taxes were $475,000; in the next year, $516,000; and last year, $540,000, a continual increase. The figures for hired labour are as follows: $2,756,000; then, it went up to $3,168,000 and in 1953 dropped back to almost the 1951 point, $2,754,000. Then, we have interest on indebtedness, and I think these are significant figures. In 1951 it was $316,000; next year it rose to $325,000; and last year it was $346,000. The cost of tractors increased from $324,000 to $415,000 and then to $469,000. The cost of fertilizer increased from $1,962,000 to $2,684,000, and last year it was $2,844,000. The figures for building repairs are as follows: in 1951, $1,075,000; 1952, $1,358,000 and last year $1,425,000. There is a steady increase in that item.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, Whether my hon. friend would object to reading now what I said about the potato crop?

I am sorry; I had intended to refer to that. I have it marked in his speech, and I thank the minister for having mentioned it. At page 4281 of Hansard the Minister of Agriculture made reference to the situation regarding the potato growers of Canada. He said:
I think I should say a few words with regard to potatoes. There has been a situation in Canada recently which is quite different from that to which we have been accustomed. We are finding it more difficult to sell our potatoes in Canada than we have done for some little time. We had to sell our potatoes at the level which has been set under the measures we took from time to time to establish floor prices. We had to establish a price in relation to potatoes grown in the maritime provinces part of which are exported, and we have not been able to hold that price at the level which was established earlier, with the result that there is a possibility that the government may have to take some loss in connection with potatoes this year.
In fairness I wish to point that out-and I could quote further if the Minister of Agriculture wishes-to express our appreciation of the potato growers of the maritime provinces generally, and of my province in particular. Perhaps I should not say that I speak for the other maritime provinces, because they may not agree with me in this;

but I do appreciate the effort which has been made by the federal government to stabilize the price of potatoes.
I cite these figures, not to be unnecessarily critical of the minister or of any other individual, but to try to bring to the attention of the public the fact that agriculture is not in a healthy condition in my province. I would like every citizen in this country to realize the seriousness of the situation, when agriculture is not healthy in every part of the country. This is particularly true of Prince Edward Island because we depend almost entirely on agriculture for our income. Of course we do have considerable income from the fishing industry as well as from the tourist industry; but those three combined are about the total. We have nothing to fall back upon worth speaking about.
Therefore when our agricultural industry is not prosperous it has a very depressing effect on our whole economy down in that province. The result is that debt increases; and it is a fact that the farmers in my province are continually going out of business. As farmers who have farmed all their lives reach the age of retirement, in many cases their farms are not turned over to the young men, or are not operated even by neighbouring farmers. They just become abandoned land.
They were leaving the farms in good times, not only in your province but in Ontario as well. In good times they have been leaving the farms and going into industry.
That is true; it is a general situation.

And
it is not any worse in the maritimes than elsewhere.

I am not suggesting that it is. I am only saying the situation does exist in the maritimes, and in my province in particular. I think it is unfortunate because, as farms become abandoned, they place heavier carrying charges on the remaining operators, especially in connection with community facilities such as power, telephones, schools, churches and the like. I do not think there can be a healthy agricultural community made up of patches of large farms with abandoned areas in between.
It has been said that the farmers have been gouging the consumer for food, and the consumer is paying an unnecessarily high price for his food. It is said that the cost of living is going up unnecessarily, and that this is partly due to increased food costs. My contention is that the agricultural industry has made itself more efficient over

the last few years at a rate which cannot be matched in many other industries-indeed, if it can be matched in any others. The average farmer is producing more per acre and per man than ever before, and the Canadian people are buying food at a smaller expense, so far as the farmer is concerned, than they ever had before. But there are other factors. The costs of processing and distribution have gone up alarmingly. Part of that is due to the fact that people want their food processed and canned, and practically ready to eat, when they take it off the grocer's shelves, whereas a number of years ago they purchased their food more in the raw state, and had to do more preparation at home before it was ready to eat.
I should like to point out that when a person buys a meal in a restaurant or eats a meal at home which has been purchased at a grocery store, the farmer gets an extremely small slice of the total cost. The mounting costs of food are due to the costs of processing and distribution. These costs may be justified, but they should be explained. And it should be explained to the Canadian people that the high cost of food is not because of the price the farmer is getting for it-in many cases, at any rate.
This was brought home to me forcibly by a friend of mine who was an official in my province of the Department of Agriculture. He attended a conference here in Ottawa last year, and while travelling to Ottawa he and his wife went into the dining car to have dinner. He said, "I was faced with a dilemma because most people quote prices in dollars-and that is fair enough, of course- but we in Prince Edward Island have come to think of potatoes as our official medium of exchange. It is from potatoes we have to earn our living. So when we went into the dining car I was faced with the problem of whether to buy a fifteen-bushel meal for myself and my wife or a twenty-bushel meal. We settled for a fifteen-bushel meal and I gave the waiter a three-peck tip, when I left.
The point is that the Canadian consumer is getting excellent value for the amount of his money that gets through to the primary producer, and the primary producer is more efficient than he has ever been before. But he is squeezed between lower prices on the one hand and rising costs on the other. He has to be efficient to survive. Competition is keener in the agricultural industry than perhaps in any other industry in the country; and anyone who is not efficient just cannot compete. It is important that the Canadian consumer be made to realize that, and I think it would be advisable if advertising were done by the Department of Agriculture, and
Supply-Agriculture
perhaps by the industry, or various segments of it, to make people realize the excellent value they are getting for their food dollar.
Perhaps because of high-pressure advertising Canadian people have been led to believe that they should get the necessities of life cheaply. This is especially true of food. They expect to get those necessities so cheaply that they can save enough money to buy the luxuries that are pushed at them through high-pressure advertising in the press, and over the radio and television. Canadians will pay 35 cents or more for a quart of beer, but they will complain if the price of a quart of milk increases from 21 cents to 22 cents. And so it is, all down the line. The Canadian people should be disabused of this notion they have that the high cost of food is owing to the farmer gouging. That is not so. The Canadian farmer is more efficient than he has ever been before. He is more efficient than his opposite number in almost any industry. I would say to the Canadian people that when they complain about the high cost of food they should analyse the cost and see what causes it, and not jump to the conclusion that it is the farmer who is getting the benefit, because it is not always so. I do not think the farmer is getting his fair share of the benefits that come from his produce.
In that connection I should like to recommend to the Canadian people a brief quotation from Artemus Ward, and also to other people who read statistics and are exposed to them from time to time. He said:
It ain't so much the things we don't know that get us in trouble. It's the things we know that ain't so.

We have had a very thorough discussion in this house on the wheat marketing problem. While I recognize the importance of a satisfactory solution to that problem, and sympathize with the growers of wheat, I want to take about five minutes to bring to the minister's attention the particular problems that face the fruit growers of the interior of British Columbia.
I am quite sure the minister cannot complain about the amount of talking that has been done on behalf of the fruit growers during this session.
Or elsewhere.

Or elsewhere; quite correct. I think they are quite modest in the representations through their organizations, and the members representing fruit growing constituencies confine their remarks to the necessary comments.
I particularly wish to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the fruit growers of

Supply-Agriculture
British Columbia, as a result of organization, and particularly good leadership, have done all they can within the limitations of present legislation, provincial and federal, to help themselves. This has been their policy all along. They believe in self-help, in doing all they can for themselves, and I am sure the minister will agree with that statement. I want to mention, particularly, the leadership at this time. We have been most fortunate in British Columbia in the leadership of the fruit growers organizations. At the present time we have Mr. Garrish, president of the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, who as a grower has had a long experience in production and wide knowledge of fruit marketing problems; Mr. A. K. Loyd, chairman of Tree Fruits Limited, is a grower of long experience, with very extensive knowledge also of domestic and international marketing problems so far as fruit is concerned. Then we have Mr. L. R. Stevens, secretary-manager of the Okanagan Federated Shippers. He has a particular knowledge of marketing and also a particular knowledge of the application of dumping duties, particularly with respect to the soft fruits and their effect upon the growers' income in British Columbia. The growers of British Columbia want the government to do what they can to help them to help themselves in two particular respects at this time.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the British Columbia fruit growers operate in the farthest north section of this continent for apple and soft fruit production on a commercial scale. In fact, British Columbia is between 400 miles and 500 miles north of the centre of the United States soft fruit producing area. That presents a particular problem for the soft fruit producers of British Columbia. This means that weeks before British Columbia fruits and vegetables appear on the Canadian market the California product is being shipped into the western Canada markets and providing the Canadian consumers with an opportunity to do their canning often quite early in the summer. I maintain, the growers maintain and their leaders maintain that for this reason alone British Columbia fruit growers believe they are entitled to particular and careful consideration in the application of dumping duties; that is the day to day situation must be watched very carefully. I see I have the support of the hon. member for Kootenay East in this respect.
They do not believe in the government permitting unfair competition when Canadian crops are in good supply. That is all they are asking for. The government should watch this dumping situation very closely
IMr. Herridge.]
and see that dumping duties are applied in a flexible way in the interests of the British Columbia fruit growers when Canadian production is in good supply. Sixty per cent of Canada's imports of fruit and vegetables come in duty free; so U. S. producers have a fair situation in that regard as far as the quantity admitted from the United States is concerned. Potatoes are free for forty-six weeks of the year, and then pay a duty of $7.50 a ton for the rest of the year. On the other hand, the United States have a tariff of $7.50 the year round against potato imports, and if the quota of table potatoes is over 1 million bushels, I am informed that the tariff is then raised to $15. I think we have been particularly fair in this respect.
I want also to bring to the attention of the minister another fact to illustrate how the growers of British Columbia have tried to help themselves. It may interest the members of the committee to know that the fruit industry in British Columbia was the only section of agriculture in Canada which, prior to the Geneva conference on trade and tariffs, got Canadian and United States interests together and decided on a course of marketing action to the advantage of the growers of both countries. As the result of consultation, common sense and a degree of compromise in that regard, I am informed there was agreement to ship a certain quantity and variety of apples particularly to eastern markets. That is a trend that should be developed. This action is an excellent demonstration of what can be done, when producing groups on both . sides of the line get together and face their common problems.
In addition to urging very careful consideration of the necessity for the application of flexible dumping duties at the right time, the fruit growers of British Columbia want the government to give particular attention to taking every advantage of every opportunity to get our fruit into the United Kingdom market again. While they appreciate the difficulties of the United Kingdom government, the increase of apple production in the United Kingdom, and the fact that the growing of certain varieties that we have been in the habit of growing in previous years, has affected the British Columbia growers market. We urge the minister to do all he can to secure a market in the United Kingdom for even a few million boxes of apples. The recapture of a portion of the United Kingdom market would have a most beneficial effect upon the tree fruit industry in British Columbia and I understand the maritimes. We grow certain varieties of apples in British Columbia to

better advantage than they can be grown anywhere else on the North American continent. The Cox Orange is grown better in British Columbia than anywhere else on the North American continent, because of certain climatic conditions. We also have other varieties, Newtown pippins and other varieties of that type, that are popular in Great Britain that we grow to particular advantage. On behalf of the growers organizations I do urge the minister and his officials to do everything they can to recapture some of the market for Canadian apples in Great Britain.

Mr. Chairman, this question of the importation of potatoes has, I am fully aware, been discussed by me in the throne speech when I first raised the question and later on when I asked questions about it. In view of the fact that recent representations have been sent to the Minister of Agriculture and others I feel that I must heartily endorse what the hon. member who has just spoken said. While I do not find myself too often on the same side as the hon. member for Kootenay East, I see that we are in agreement on this question at least. We must try to give a certain measure of protection to this industry if it is going to continue.
At this particular time I should like to draw a note to the attention of the minister that appeared in the Country Guide of April, 1954, of a different tenor. It is not too amusing when one considers its far-reaching implications. The heading is, "The Disguised Potato". The article says in part:
Capping it all is the "Case of the Disguised Potato", which is causing agricultural sleuths a good deal of concern on the local markets. United States shippers have been trying to pull a fast one on British Columbia housewives by offering an "early, red-skinned" potato that showed a remarkable talent for sprouting when displayed on the stands. Investigation revealed them to be old-crop, white-skinned potatoes which had been dyed red and then waxed to give that new-potato look. Potatoes with make-up! Shades of Max Factor-what won't they think of next!
Well, they certainly have the new look if they are red. You can understand the feelings of many British Columbia housewives who thought they were buying new potatoes and discovered they had bought potatoes with make-up. I think that potatoes should not be allowed to come in in disguise, and certainly they should not appear in that condition on the market and be sold to housewives as new potatoes.
As regards the other matter of importation duty, I would strongly urge the minister to discuss with the Minister of National Revenue the desirability of trying to get the act changed in time for next session because I am sure such a change would meet with 83276-393
Supply-Agriculture
universal approval, and certainly we would support it. That change should embody a more elastic provision. Such tariff should come into force when the second early potatoes come in from the United States. This would certainly seem to remedy the difficulty. Our British Columbia early potato growers have their potatoes arriving on the market when the second earlies from the United States come on our market, with the result that the United States first earlies are put on the British Columbia market at a dumping price. Unfortunately, that dumping price is not one that can be considered as such because the United States has dropped the price on their home market, and therefore this does not come within the dumping regulations. Other potatoes are not yet on sale, and having been stored they have that greenish look. The result is that when they are put on the market they merely cut down the price to which the British Columbia grower is legitimately entitled for his first early potatoes and he is placed in the unfair position of having to compete with the United States product.
Now, another product which comes in under a similar category is the turkey. We believe that the turkey raisers have a legitimate complaint and we think they should have some further protection on the turkey market. We find that the consumption of United States turkeys in Canada has increased considerably because our industry is not getting the form of protection to which it feels it is entitled. One might ask why United States turkeys are being permitted into this country and how the United States turkey producers can raise and sell them so much more cheaply if the price of feed and other grain is the same as it is in Canada. The reason for it is that in the state of Oregon, for example, the banks own a large number of these ranches by way of loan and they force the turkey raisers to sell their turkeys and flood the market from time to time by giving notice that they intend to recall their loan, with the result that these producers have to sell their turkeys in the nearest market which is accessible, and that happens to be the Canadian market. In certain areas we find our own markets being flooded with birds being dumped from across the border, although they cost the United States consumers the same price; and that is where our difficulty originates. The effect of that is felt by the grain growers of Canada. They probably have not thought of this angle, though I think it is worth considering.
Last year about 250,000 United States birds were sent into Canada. The consumption of that number of birds would indirectly affect the use of five million bushels of feed grain.

Supply-Agriculture
Now, five million bushels of wheat and other grains is not a tremendous amount out of our colossal surplus of 700 million bushels, and I quite realize that, but at the same time every five million bushels helps and we know that these imported birds consume that amount of grain.
I hope the minister will use his influence with the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance, in considering the problem of potatoes and turkeys, to see whether we cannot have a greater amount of protection for the British Columbia industry.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order: I do not wish to interfere with the desire of hon. members to express themselves at this stage, but of the last two speeches one has dealt with fruit and the other with potatoes and turkeys, and I think it would be better if we could withhold the discussion on these matters until we come to the items covering them. I know it has always been customary to allow a general discussion on the condition of agriculture, but when it comes to dealing with such things as the sale of turkeys and fruit I think we should reserve that until we come to the item dealing with them so that I can give whatever information is available and deal with questions in a manner which would be helpful. I am suggesting that, and I hope hon. members who have something to say about a particular item will reserve their remarks until that item is called.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the subject of wheat would be relevant to this discussion. My name has been mentioned by the last two hon. members who have spoken and they have indicated that they support me, perhaps more than I support them, in the matter of dumping duties and tariffs on soft fruits and vegetables at this time of the year. I want to say that I certainly support the plea for protection on behalf of our growers who supply fresh fruit and early vegetables, not only because a tariff is necessary to protect them at this time but because I know that their products are of superior quality when they reach the market. A large number of people are inveigled into buying products that are old and somewhat withered although they might appear to be new vegetables.
On the other hand, just yesterday I received a telegram from a hospital society in my riding which wanted to know why a duty was put on new potatoes at this time while they were unable to obtain that product on the local market or from British Columbia producers. I took this matter up and I understand it is an automatic impost having

regard to the fact that there are fluctuations in the seasons, and for that reason it is statutory and also prevents the suppliers from stocking up and selling at a later date as fresh vegetables the products which have been harvested some time before.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he be in favour of my proposal that the government refrain from imposing this duty until United States secondaries come in? That, to my mind, would assure that Canadian first earlies would be available for this hospital.

I think that is probably a reasonable suggestion. As I said, my riding is so diversified that it is difficult to know just what is going to work in the best interest of the entire area. It might be interesting just at this point to tell you that last fall I was asked by the miners' union to journey to St. Louis, Missouri, to speak on the resolution that was being presented to the government of the United States asking that they do not introduce any further tariffs on lead and zinc. I gladly took that opportunity and I know that the resolution passed unanimously. I therefore cannot come out too strongly-after that decision which I think was the right one-and ask that impositions be put on materials and foodstuffs that the working people are required to purchase. However, I think there is a happy medium that we can reach. I think the farmer and the industrial worker must appraise their various situations and see that one does nothing that is going to injure the other. It is for that reason that I am on my feet on this occasion.
In the past few days, Mr. Chairman, we have had a great deal of discussion during which the opposition, and more particularly the C.C.F. opposition, have asked us to put a floor price on wheat. Such a floor price, in effect, at some stage or other would mean a subsidy. Reference has been made to a $65 million payment which was made by this parliament some years ago and which I voted to grant. While no one admits that it was a subsidy, however we may look at it, in effect it was a grant in lieu of certain payments which the farmers felt should have been made. They maintain that their price was stabilized at a certain given period and that they could have received a higher price if it had not been stabilized. But of course those who speak only for the farmers neglect to remind the House of Commons that for many years industrial wages were stabilized and that the prices of industrial products were stabilized. For instance, in the particular industry in which I work, all during the war

there was one set price. Almost at the opening of the war a price was set. The product remained at that price throughout the war and the wages of the people working in that industry remained almost static. It is for this reason that I say we want to work together and that no one should do or say anything that is going to injure the other.
On December 2 of last year I took exception to a statement that had been made by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. I regret that he is not in his seat at the moment. However, we cannot pick and choose our time for making these replies but must make them as the opportunity presents itself at any given time. I took exception to the statement that he made with regard to the price of fertilizer. I think I can relate this question of fertilizer closely to the price and the cost of production of this extremely important product that we have been discussing for the past few days, namely, wheat. As with any other product, if you raise 20 bushels to the acre it costs you a certain figure, having regard to the cost of the seed, the wear and tear on machinery, the over-all cost of the land itself and of harvesting. It costs almost as much to raise 20 bushels as it does to raise 40 bushels. That fact has been brought out in the house, I think. I know that on a recent trip to the west I visited in southern Alberta and discussed this matter with some farmers. They said that the crops they have had during the last three years have not cost them nearly as much to produce -that is, per bushel-as did the crops during the previous ten years. They therefore could conceive of receiving a lower price without there being any such catastrophe as has been indicated here, or without any disastrous effect on their economy as a result of receiving a slightly lower price. When I say this I am going to give some advice, perhaps. Even if I had not had some experience in the growing of wheat, I would consider myself qualified to do so after sitting here for the last five years and hearing the discussions, which are many, with regard to this question.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort indicated that the fertilizer industry was gouging the farmers.

Hear,
hear.

He indicated that the cost of
fertilizer was almost double or three times what it was in relation to wheat in 1939. The hon. member says "hear, hear".
There, there.

The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort said that the figure 1 gave of 83276-3931

100,000 tons of fertilizer being used on the prairie provinces in 1953 gave an increased production of 35 million bushels was incorrect. The hon. member maintained that the most this could amount to would be 15 million bushels. Incidentally, he said that these figures are from the dominion bureau of statistics and cannot be denied. My purpose in rising today then is to deny that very statement he has made.
One hundred thousand tons of fertilizer will fertilize about 5 million acres, at the recommended amount of 40 pounds to the acre. With the hon. member's figure of 15 million bushels, this would amount to an average increase of about 3 bushels to the acre, or less, having regard to the amount applied in different areas. It would be extremely difficult for a sales manager of a fertilizer company to convince the farmer that this increase would be of very great assistance to him.
The hon. member stated that these were figures from the dominion bureau of statistics, taken, of course, from the experiments of the federal experimental farms. I do not know how the figures became so twisted but it is possible that the plots used by the dominion experimental farm would be areas that have been from time to time built up- that is, the soil itself would be built up-to such a condition, because of crop rotation and so forth, that the introduction of fertilizer would not have a great effect. I have here a report of the Dominion of Canada information service, No. E-97, on the subject of fertilizers for northeastern Saskatchewan. The report was released on March 22, 1954, and reads in part as follows:
Ammonium phosphate 11-48-0 has been applied to cereal crops grown on summer fallow at the experimental station at Melfort for the past 14 years. Agronomist B. K. McDonald says a summary of these results on Melfort silty clay soil for wheat has shown an average yield increase of 6 0 bushels per acre for wheat, 12-5 bushels for barley and 8-2 bushels for oats when the 40 pound rate of 11-48-0 was used. These yield increases have given net returns of $5.50 per acre for wheat, $6 for barley and $2 for oats.
Now an hon. member stated that these statistics cannot be denied. I wonder if he would take the word of the University of Saskatchewan and accept the results they give in a table I have here with respect to the use of a similar type of fertilizer. This circular was issued uy the department of soils, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, in February, 1952. A rate of application of 25 pounds per acre in 1941, a dry year, produced a result of 2-8, and in 1942, a moist year, a result of 11-3. The average from 1939 to 1943 was 7-9 bushels. That of course is for wheat.
