Would the hon. member indicate where that test was made?

If you will allow me, I will
finish this table first. A rate of application of 50 pounds per acre showed an increase of 4-5 bushels in 1941, a dry year, 13-4 bushels in 1942, a moist year, and from 1939 to 1943 the average was 10-2 bushels per acre. These tests were made in various areas throughout Saskatchewan. They were not in any one particular plot.
The first one was at Melfort. Would you indicate where the second one was?

There are several distinct areas. But I have figures showing an even better yield from other areas. This is on summer-fallow in Saskatchewan in the dark brown area. I am sure the hon. member knows more about the areas of Saskatchewan than I do. I know one of course very well, Maple Creek, the area from which the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek comes. Perhaps some would attack the use of fertilizers for large crops there in a very dry and sandy soil. However, the hon. member knows the areas better than I do. In the dark brown soil zone 71 tests made with a 20-pound application produced an increase of 4 bushels per acre, and with a 40-pound application 5-5 bushels per acre. In the black soil zone 83 tests showed an increase of 5-2 bushels with a 20-pound application and an increase of 7-2 bushels with a 40-pound application. There is another area called the degraded black and grey soil zone. With a 20-pound application there was an increase of 4 bushels per acre and with a 40-pound application an increase of 6-2 bushels.
Forty pounds to the acre?

Forty pounds to the acre. In saying this I want it to be understood that I want to co-operate in every way to assist the farmers. There are a large number of farmers in my own riding. But I do think that the facts should be kept straight. In that way we can assist one another. If the fertilizer industry continues to expand, as I hope it will-and I see no reason why it should not-if the farmers are acquainted with the facts and are desirous of raising the largest amount of grain or other products they can on the smallest acreage, then they will be able to do so by making use of fertilizer.
I am sure the house would be interested to know something about the situation in Kimberley where this fertilizer is made. At the present time one unit is supplying the market, but there is a potential market on

the prairies four times what we have now. This one unit leaves a residue, from the processing of iron sulphides, of about 200 tons of pig iron daily when it reduces the iron tailings from the Sullivan mine to produce sulphuric acid for the production of fertilizer. I had the interesting experience of visiting the laboratory of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys the other day and I saw steel being made out of this pig iron. On a second trip I saw the steel being rolled out, and from all appearances it is going to be the finest of steel. Of course that requires a good deal of experimentation, but it is hoped that we will be able to make steel of the very finest grade.
We hope to expand the industry and by so doing we will be able to pay more taxes and provide more jobs. If a subsidy should become necessary for certain farm products we will certainly be glad to pay it, but I say: Live and let live. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort also said when he was home at Christmas his neighbours were pledging themselves by way of a petition to refuse to buy fertilizer. I do not know whether or not the hon. member signed the petition. I suppose it was a bit unfair to delve into this matter further, but the hon. member said that he had delved into my figures so I took the opportunity to examine his. I find that despite the fact that such a petition was circulated in that area .asking the farmers not to buy fertilizer, a syndicate known as Cariboo Farms, and I believe owned by Bryson Brothers, took delivery of 11 tons of fertilizer this spring. If the hon. member encouraged other farmers to sign the petition and signed it himself he nevertheless did not see fit to abstain from buying this material, which apparently gives pretty fair results.
There is another matter that I should like to discuss at this time, the question of the extension of the P.F.R.A. into the province of British Columbia. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, as the name implies, provides assistance only in the prairie provinces. Now, British Columbia's population is rapidly expanding, and we hope it will continue to do so. We have some extremely arid areas in the province. Recently, of course, as on the prairie provinces, there has been sufficient rain to grow hay crops and so on, but the rainfall is not dependable. I feel that in order to supply this ever-expanding population we should have this very fertile soil under irrigation. We have other areas also, of course, that are in need of reclamation. I see no reason why, now that we have these very large wheat surpluses, we should not look towards the development of other crops. Certainly in British Columbia, where we

have a much longer growing season, we could undertake more diversified crops. There is no argument against giving assistance, as has been done on the prairies. I am looking forward to having the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act changed at an early date to omit the word "prairie" and make it just the farm rehabilitation act.

I wonder whether the minister could indicate if he has reports concerning the flood damage in northeastern Saskatchewan during recent weeks, and if so the extent of the damage done? My information is that seeding was delayed for a very long time, and that flood damage has been very serious over quite an extended area. I would appreciate it if he could make some statement as to the extent of the damage, and whether any benefits might be available to the people in the area under federal legislation?
Going back to what I said a few moments ago, I will be in a position to do that when we get to the item covering it, but not on this general item.

The other matter I was going to raise concerns policy, and I think perhaps this would be the appropriate time to take a minute to do so. I do not plan on reopening the wheat debate. An editorial in the Leader-Post the other day suggested that wheat production is still profitable at the prevailing price, and what is more, farmers could augment their returns from feed grains by feeding livestock and selling them on the hoof instead of selling the grain. I am sure the western farmers will appreciate that free advice, as will eastern farmers.
However, if that advice is to be taken seriously, the minister should give some indication that the government is prepared to stand by somewhere along the line. The Leader-Post also mentioned that the request made here in parliament would entail an average annual handout of probably $50 million per year to the Canadian wheat producers.

I think if we are ever going to get through with this discussion we have to have some rules. The marketing of wheat does not come under this department at all. It has been discussed now for several days and I do not think we should discuss it again on the estimates of this department because this department does not handle the marketing of wheat.

No, I am aware of that. I am saying that if farmers have to go into livestock, the government should indicate that livestock prices are not going to go down the way they did during the thirties. I may
Supply-Agriculture
say that during my sojourn on the farm I acted on some advice the minister gave from time to time that it would be a good idea to sell some of the damp and tough grain back in 1951 as livestock. We therefore bought from one of our neighbours his herd of cattle, and we have had the company of those cattle now for three years. I was just checking the prices listed by the bureau of statistics the other day, and I find that the price in November, 1951, for medium cows was $23.07, and in this year it is $11.56; for yearlings, common, $13.50 now and in 1951, $29.46.
The point I am making is that if our neighbour would like to have those cattle back now we could give him two head for every one we got from him, and we would not charge him anything for the feed or for the company of the cattle during that period. If he should buy them back and keep them for another two or three years, I wonder if at the end of that time he would need to sell us twice as many as he is getting. We have had very good luck with cattle, but I think the government should indicate at some point whether or not they are going to give some protection to farmers in all parts of Canada. If there is not going to be a floor for grain a very large number of farmers are going to be obliged to go into livestock. It is quite possible there may be a further drop in the price of livestock. Could the minister indicate, even if he is not prepared to give some assurance, that if a large volume of this grain goes into cattle or pigs the bottom will not drop out of the cattle market altogether?

I just wanted to say a word or two of a general nature on this matter. Perhaps the point at which the hon. member for Mackenzie stopped is as good a one as any for me to start, because I intended to ask the minister if, during the course of his estimates, he would say a word about departmental policy with respect to livestock marketing. The figures given by the hon. member for Mackenzie give an indication of the general experience across the whole of the country. They vary a little from market to market and they may not be necessarily in accordance with the present price in Vancouver, where our livestock is marketed in the main, but they indicate the experience we have been having in British Columbia. Our experience has been that during the last two years cattle prices have been halved; actually, it is a decline of 100 per cent although it depends upon which end you start from. Some might say it is 50 per cent decline.
Inasmuch as farmers' costs have not come down-at least, I have not any accurate

Supply-Agriculture
figures to show whether they have gone up or remained stationary, but by and large I think it would be correct to say they are the same, if not higher than they were two years ago. It will be seen that the substantial decline in price represents a serious problem to the livestock producers of British Columbia. They would like to hear from the minister some forecast of the government's policy with respect to livestock marketing.
Unfortunately, I am not able at this time to discuss the problem with respect to grading, as I should like to do, but I suggest there are certain weaknesses in the grading system. These weaknesses result in a very large spread between the returns to the farmers for the cattle in comparison with what the packers get for the different grades themselves. I have on the order paper a resolution which precludes me from going into detail on that matter at this time, although I hope next year to follow up that resolution and have a discussion of the problem. Perhaps the minister might say a word or two on that subject when he deals with the general one, as I hope he will, of the government's policy with regard to the marketing of livestock.
I should like to say just a word or two in support of what was said by the hon. member for New Westminster in connection with the potato situation. I will keep my remarks quite general; but I think it is proper to make them here because this is a problem requiring co-operation between this department and the Department of National Revenue.
In the constituency I represent, the potato growers operate under two different marketing boards, depending upon where they are. But, by and large, in the Kamloops and Ashcroft districts they operate under the interior vegetable board, whereas in the Pemberton district, with which the minister is particularly familiar they operate under the coast vegetable marketing board. But the problems of marketing and the difficulties with which they are confronted, as a result of the importation of American potatoes, are very much the same.
When I was down at Pemberton last summer they told me it was a great pity that the benefits which it had been expected would be derived from the extensive and generally successful reclamation works carried on by the Department of Agriculture under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration were not being realized because of the difficulties they were having in marketing their potatoes.
The solution seems largely to lie in an intelligent and flexible application of the

seasonal duties against the importation of American potatoes. I suggest a fixed seasonal duty is not of much value in assisting our growers because of the difference from season to season in the period during which potatoes come on the market. From year to year the season varies, and the time at which our potatoes come on would be as early in some cases as July or the end of June, whereas in other years they would not come on until well into July, or perhaps August. I do not know whether my dates are exactly correct, but I mention these dates to point out the variation in the dates in which potatoes are offered as between one part of the riding and another.
If a protective seasonal duty is fixed absolutely it will not take account of seasonal climatic variations between one year and another. I would therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture if he would bring the influence of his department to bear on the Department of National Revenue so as to have the application of that protective measure made more flexible.
My understanding is that at the present time it is fixed by statute and, as such, it is not of much benefit to us. I do not think it would have any adverse effect either on consumers or on American producers if it were made more flexible. It would simply enable the growers to take account of seasonal variations from year to year.
I have had telegrams-and I am sure other hon. members on both sides of the house in all parties, including the minister have also had them-indicating that this year, because of the lateness of the season, the protection fixed by statute coming into effect on certain fixed dates is not going to be of any assistance to them. I am hoping therefore that we might be able to persuade the government to amend the act so as to provide for a flexible period, but at no higher rates. We are not asking for higher rates; we are asking only that the season during which these rates are applicable be made more flexible. I would hope the minister would give some indication as to whether his department can make any progress with the Department of National Revenue along these lines. I hope he will be able to say something which will reassure the producers of livestock who, in my section of the country at any rate, are very much concerned as a result of the decline in prices- a decline which has not been accompanied by a corresponding decline in their costs of production.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should say just a word on this matter of potatoes. A resolution did come in about a week ago from British Columbia-I do not

remember the exact date-suggesting that the dates, which now stand at June 15 to August 1, should be changed to July 1 to August 15. I have had that matter submitted to our officials and have asked them to take it up with other departments to see what can be done about it.
I am somewhat surprised to hear that these things are set by statute, because such matters are submitted to me from time to time for my opinion. If they are controlled by statute I do not see how my opinion could have much effect.
However, I shall look into the matter. We now have it under consideration, and we will see what can be done about it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks at this time regarding the value of extended research in the agricultural industry. As most of us know, agriculture is still the backbone of our Canadian economy, and this economy to a very large extent is dependent upon the farmer as the greatest consumer of the products of industrial labour.
It certainly follows that any reduction in farm income will be felt by way of reduced incomes of people living in cities and towns. Figures offered by hon. members have shown that farm income has been reduced in the east by approximately 35 per cent and in the west by about 15 per cent in the last several years. This would seem to be an average reduction of income of about 25 per cent.
Cheap food and a high level of employment do not go together at all. Any depression, which nowadays, I believe, we call a recession, is always preceded-at least that has been so in the past-by a mounting surplus of agricultural products. This is well exemplified in Canada at the present time by the very large surplus of wheat and by a surplus of milk products.
I think we have to face these facts in order that we shall not repeat some of the mistakes we made in the past. At the present time, despite government statements to the contrary, there is little doubt that many of us would agree that Canada is at present still faced with a rather dangerous economic situation. I should like just for a few minutes to make a few remarks to indicate what has led up to this potentially dangerous economic situation-and I shall not describe it as a crisis. We can go back a little while to cost-plus government contracts, necessary as they may have been in the production of implements of war, and describe them as probably the greatest single factor in starting the long inflationary spiral
Supply-Agriculture
of prices which brought about increased wages, increased costs, increased taxes and demands for subsidies.
I believe we would all agree that the current problem facing agriculture today could be solved if some way could be devised to get rid of the surpluses of farm products now piling up in Canada and-this is equally important-in the United States. It is quite true that international markets indicate a demand for farm products, but they also are faced with the problem of little or no money, with the result that farm surpluses both here and in the United States are simply not moving into the markets where they should be moving.
This problem was recognized a few years ago when it was suggested that a fund be established under the United Nations to provide for the distribution of surplus agricultural production, under the United Nations, to countries where these products were needed. This was then and certainly is today a very good idea. But unfortunately it is one which it is very difficult to implement. As a result, nothing has been done about it. I have heard people argue this point-and I suppose it can be argued in the present instance-that there has never been a true surplus of farm products in the world because there have always been people without enough food. But the fact remains that huge surpluses are now piling up on this continent, and are having a disastrous effect upon our economy-and will have an even more disastrous effect in the future.
The basic problem is not only whether other nations want or need our food or whether or not our farmers can produce it- they certainly can-but whether or not people in those other countries can pay for it and pay for it in some form of currency that we can use. It is this problem which has had such a devastating effect upon our most stable export markets in the past and which I am sure is evidenced by the record of our lost markets in the United Kingdom. Here in Canada our comparatively small population, combined with the high fertility of our soil, gives us a very heavy dependence on export markets. We have found by experience many times in our short history that one of the major problems in building dependable export markets for foodstuffs is the ease with which most importer countries can either do without, buy elsewhere, or themselves increase their domestic food production.
Take as an example our market for agricultural products in the United Kingdom. For years Canadian farmers were the largest

Supply-Agriculture
exporters ol food products into the British markets, selling as they did the big proportion of their imports of oats, wheat, wheat flour, bacon, cheese, condensed milk, apples, salmon, lumber and many other products. From supplying 96 per cent of their total imports of oats, 27 per cent of their total imports of beans, 43 per cent of their total imports of beef and 83 per cent of their total imports of bacon, today we sell hardly any of these products and the volume of our exports has also been seriously reduced.
True, it made good economic sense for Canada to produce large quantities of a variety of food products to supply the British market, but the bald fact is that economic considerations of national importance to the United Kingdom have made it difficult for them to buy from us and pay for it in currency we could use; in other words, it is the sterling problem which has been mentioned so often in this house. Nor could we as a nation, much as we desire to help other countries and especially the United Kingdom, be expected continually to give away our products whether by direct gifts of money or as produce. The economic realities of this fact were clearly expressed by both countries, the United States and the United Kingdom, as one of trade, not aid.
Our experience in selling farm products in the British market conclusively proves another problem confronting agriculture and that is that, for many reasons, economic considerations do not have the same practical effect on the international trade in foodstuffs as they do on trade in other materials. We find that barter deals, bulk buying, price supports and other devices really do not give any assurance of stability of markets for the producer.
As we lost the British market for our primary producers, we were able during and after the war to find export outlets in the United States, and this was also accompanied by a highly speeded-up increase in home consumption. High levels of employment in Canada resulted in greater demand at home for the produce of our farms. This, coupled with the increased exports to the United States, meant that for a while the full impact of the loss of British markets was not felt.
Today, however, we are confronted with the unpleasant fact that these alternative markets are rapidly dwindling. High costs of production in Canada, due to high taxes, higher wage levels than in countries competing with Canadian textile industry and others, such as Japan, Belgium, Germany and so on, have made it increasingly difficult to sell our manufactured goods both abroad and at home. The Minister of Labour has not given

out the most recent figures of those seeking jobs, but the ones that were available a month ago indicated that there were over half a million persons still seeking jobs in Canada, which is a much higher number than those seeking jobs in other years, not to mention those on short work weeks, which has reduced the earning power for the industrial worker and has accordingly seriously reduced his ability to buy not only manufactured goods but farm products as well. Here is a very important fact, and I think it ties in particularly with the Canadian situation.
Increasing surpluses in the United States, arising in part at least from the fact that they too have lost export markets abroad, have resulted in embargoes being placed against imports of agricultural products from Canada. Our alternative market for dairy products formerly sold in the United Kingdom was shut out by the United States embargo against their import. This was later followed by our government's voluntary agreement with the United States to restrict our export of oats to that country until October, 1954, when the situation will be reviewed.
Like Canada, the United States today is confronted with a tremendous surplus of primary products for which there appears no immediate export market. It is expected that at the end of this crop year the United States government will be holding in storage approximately $5,500,000,000 worth of surplus produce purchased by the government but at present without demand in any export markets able to pay prevailing prices for their purchases. I understand that in the United States of course they have schemes for subsidizing exports to help matters at home, but I do not think that has any particular effect on the basic principle and the basic danger involved. Indications point to a desire by the government of the United States to distribute some of these huge surpluses to other countries under its system of aid to combat communist aggression. We have seen examples of that in the past. This of course increases the difficulty of selling our farm products abroad because if countries can get food for nothing, why pay for it? While it is not conceivable that such a policy would be followed as an accepted policy of dumping, the fact remains that whatever action is taken along this line will be adversely felt in Canada.
We are also confronted with the problem of surpluses rapidly accumulating. We have not yet sold one bushel of last year's wheat crop. If the minister is able to make some comment on that later, certainly we shall welcome it. This is only one product surplus in the United States. In addition to

that we are apparently now being faced with the possibility at least of a price war on the international wheat market, which we have heard so much about in the last few days. The question is, what will happen to the export markets we are now supplying? Can these nations be expected to buy from us at prevailing prices if the same or substitute products can be secured for less money or, as mentioned before, for no money at all elsewhere?
If we take the long-term view on a suggested solution to the problem of markets for our agricultural products, it seems to me wise for us to start and consider now how, with the exception of wheat, and possibly a few other products, the output of our agricultural industry can be largely consumed at home.
True, over the years the population of Canada will increase and steps are being taken along that line now. But what we are interested in at the moment is not something that is going to take place ten years, twenty years, thirty years or forty years from now, but something that will take place shortly. It is true that our population may be 40 million people fifty years from now, but that is not going to answer the questions confronting us at the moment. We should direct our attention now to the possibilities ahead in the field of speeded-up research to find industrial uses for Canadian agricultural products. During the last ten years we have experienced a tremendous increase of industrialization in Canada. The demand for raw materials for industry has increased to a point that would not have been imagined ten years ago. Most of these raw materials came, of course, originally from the soil. It is quite true that climatic conditions in this country prevent many of these raw materials from ever being produced in Canada. Nevertheless, the fact remains that that quantity of raw materials needed by industry could be produced by the primary producers of this country if the facts were properly made known to them. In other words, some of the land area of this country, now devoted to the production of food products, of which there is at present a surplus supply, could profitably be directed to the production of new and different crops for which available home markets do or could exist in Canada.
The reasoning behind this proposal is very simple. All over the earth man cultivates only about 1,500 species of plants. Botanists have already named over 300,000 species. In the United States, where great strides are being made to find industrial uses for agricultural productive capacity, the commercial agricultural production of that nation
Supply-Agriculture
comes from fewer than 300 species of plants and by far the most of it from fewer than 30 species, notwithstanding the fact that there are over 15,000 kinds of plants native to North America north of the Gulf of Mexico.
It is quite understandable that in the past man cultivated only a few species of plants because until the last century man was pretty well limited by what he was able to handle and utilize. Today, however, engineering science has provided machines to do work previously considered impossible and chemists have given us the means to convert various kinds of plant material into useful commodities previously unknown. Examples of this are many and obvious. But, Mr. Chairman, I see my time is running short and I do not think T will take up the time of the committee to go into the long list of examples I have here. In this country no real effort has yet been extended towards any systematic examination of species of plants that will grow in this country to determine their inherent chemical composition and potential uses.
In industry today we do not need more production of those things we now have in surplus supply and for which there appears to be no immediate export market available. But we do need more effort expended to find out how much more of the raw materials used in industry we could and should produce on the farms of this country.
I believe that this question should become a matter of study and consideration by every farm organization in Canada. Certainly, speeded-up research at government levels to find out new and profitable uses for agricultural production should be provided at once. By such action the, shall I say, productive might of the agricultural economy of this country can be directed in the way of producing those things for which available markets exist in the immediate foreseeable future.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two questions I would like to ask related to a matter I brought up last Tuesday and which caused some discussion. I want the minister to settle the matter and I think this is the only item under which I can bring the matter up. It deals with the food and agriculture organization. The minister, when he spoke on Tuesday, made it clear that he thought I had gone out of my way to try to discredit or misrepresent him on this matter. I want to make it absolutely clear to the minister that he is quite wrong in this and that there was nothing further from my mind. I have always had a very high appreciation of the work the minister has done in the interests of western Canada. I have expressed that appreciation in the house

Supply-Agriculture
and also in the constituency which I represent. But that is not to say I am not to be allowed to criticize certain policies tor which the minister is responsible, and I try to do that in a fair manner.
I want to say a few words regarding the point he raised. When I spoke last on this subject I pointed out that the minister had always supported the policies of Sir John Boyd Orr, and then I went on to point out the origin of the work the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had done, and the work the international federation of agricultural producers had done, and then I pointed out what had been done by the body of six experts appointed by the FAO council and that their proposals had nothing to do with Sir John Boyd Orr.
I then pointed out that the minister had opposed them and I said the minister voted against their proposals. That is where the minister challenged me and that is where some statements were made that had perhaps better not have been made. I thought I was being absolutely correct when I made that statement and I think I can prove I am correct.
What are you trying to prove as being correct? You quoted me as saying I had voted against it.

Merely that I was not the one who induced the minister to make the statement he did. I quoted the minister as saying he had voted against the international commodity clearing house. The minister in his speech said he was wrong in making that statement; but I was hardly responsible for that, and I did not induce the minister to make that statement. What led me to say that the minister had voted against it was the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture on previous occasions. It is not the first time the minister has stated in this house that he voted against it. Right back to 1951 the minister has been making statements of that kind, and just to make absolutely clear to the minister what he has said I will quote part of his speech as reported at page 2086 of Hansard for December 17, 1951, when the matter was under discussion. I hope the minister is not going to criticize me for not quoting his entire speech. The minister made a rather long and rambling speech on that occasion, but I will just quote part of what he said regarding this matter:
All Canada ever did in the matter was to say that it would be an impossible position for Canada to head a group of nations who would find it impossible to finance such a proposition, so Canada could not vote for something she could not possibly carry out. Canada voted against that.

That is why I jumped to the conclusion I did, though the minister has now made it clear that no vote was taken; so I will not repeat the statement that the minister voted against it.
Since then I have had an opportunity of going into the report of the council and while it is clear that no vote was taken it is nevertheless clear that the proposal was rejected. The minister in his speech from which I just quoted did say that he voted against it.
I did not.

His position at that time was that he was not going to be put in a position of supporting a proposal if that proposal was not going to be supported by the other nations, because if he did that Canada would be left holding the bag with the other nations refusing to support her. That may be a good reason. But, on the other hand, suppose the other nations had taken that attitude and said they were not going to support it because the other nations were not supporting it, and "we do not want to be left holding the bag". But that is not the reason given by the report of the conference.

May I just ask the hon. member to correct a statement he has just made. A moment ago he said he was not going to say any more that I voted against this, but in his second subsequent sentence he repeated the assertion again that I did vote against it.

No, I am merely quoting the minister as to what he said at that time and as to why I said he voted against it. I am not saying now that he voted against it. I have quoted the reasons given by the minister three years ago and I took it from that that he voted against it because he said that Canada was not going to be left holding the bag.
Just check Hansard and you will find that what I said a moment ago is correct.
That is not the reason given in the report of the conference.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 pun.

Mr. Chairman, before the lunch recess I had been referring to the international commodity clearing house and the fact that when the food and agriculture

organization conference in 1949-50 rejected the proposal of an international commodity clearing house-and let me point out that, when I say that, I am quoting the exact words of the director general in his report for 1949-50-a committee on commodity problems was set up or was appointed. I was especially interested in an article in the March, 1954, issue of Memo which is an FAO publication. The heading is "Special Measures to Dispose of Farm Surpluses Suggested". I will just quote a short paragraph:
The long-term solution to the problem of food and other farm surpluses lies in increased consumption through higher incomes and the increased demand that will result from the growth of population. A selective expansion of production and the adaptation of farm production to changing needs must also operate in the solution.
In the short-term, however, there is great need for specific action to dispose of existing supplies and to prevent new surpluses from accumulating.
This was the finding of the 8-nation working party on agricultural surpluses which met in Washington from February 23 to March 18 to explore all possible ways of dealing with the current surplus problem.
The working party urged that governments give special consideration to these five methods of surplus disposal: . . .
Then it gives the five proposals, three of which are as follows: Sales on concessional terms for three different purposes; second, sales against importers' currencies, to be used for special purposes; and third, holdings, or segregation, of stocks. I suppose it could be argued that we have already put into practice some of these proposals. We are doing some of these things today. Especially interesting is proposal No. 2. I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce sitting there. He has already expressed, I would say, almost contempt for the suggestion that anything could be accomplished by accepting other nations' currencies in payment for our surpluses. But I see that this is a recommendation that has now been made by the eight nations, and I think that Canada is one of those nations to put forward this proposal. I am therefore interested in knowing whether or not the Canadian government endorses these proposals. Personally, I think they are fine suggestions.
It is interesting to note that the United States were putting into practice the second suggestion back in 1951 under the security act and that now, under the new proposal they are making, they are proposing to go a great deal further; that is, they are proposing to accept foreign currencies and to use them not merely for the purpose of building up nations' defences but for a wide variety of purposes. If the United States are prepared
Supply-A griculture
to sell their goods on that basis, it seems to me that it is going to put us in a difficult position if we refuse to do likewise. The question I should like to ask the minister is this. Just how is a report of that kind dealt with? Will that be considered and be either accepted or rejected by a vote in the agricultural conference, or is it just a series of proposals made to the member nations, leaving it up to each individual nation to decide whether or not they want to act on those proposals, either in part or in whole, independently of one another? The minister might answer that question at his convenience.
I should now like to raise one other question which is also related to farm products, but is of an internal character. As the minister knows, there is in western Canada today a great deal of interest in the subject of marketing boards. The minister knows that in Alberta the enabling legislation was not passed largely because the government apparently was not at all sure that the farmers were in favour of such action. However, I understand that this summer a large series of meetings will be held and that an attempt will be made to get the farmers to indicate whether or not they are in favour of marketing board legislation or rather enabling legislation. If the farmers express an opinion that such action should be taken, I believe that probably a plebiscite will be taken, and provided a majority of the farmers vote in favour of the proposal, then I suppose that enabling legislation will be put into operation.
That being the situation, I can envisage that when I get back home, if I am attending any of these meetings, I am going to be asked a number of questions. I should like to get a little bit of information from the Minister of Agriculture so as to try to make sure that my answers will be correct. In the first place, am I correct in believing that, if these boards are set up, they will be entitled to a guaranteed initial payment up to possibly 80 per cent of the average price of the past three years? I believe the act provides for 80 per cent, although I understand the general practice is to make the initial guarantee up to 60 per cent. Furthermore, would they be entitled to a support price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act if the price of commodities falls to the level set by the formula under the Agricultural Prices Support Act? In that connection, is the formula that the minister explained to the house a year or so ago still in operation? Is the support price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act based upon the three base years, 1943, 1944 and 1945? If I could get an

Supply-Agriculture
answer to those questions, I think it would help a number of us in dealing with this question when we get back home.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman.
I wish to ask one or two questions of the minister with regard to professional services. There is a scientific service and an economic service. Let me say this at the outset. Although I am lamentably ignorant about science, I believe I know enough to know how important a part it plays in agricultural production. For example, my friend the hon. member for Huron this morning was pointing out to me that in his part of the world there is a blight on the cedar trees at the moment and that investigations will be going on with a view to discovering the cause and finding a cure. My question is merely this. I do not mean to suggest for a moment that there needs to be less work done. I want to ask whether there is any danger of such a thing as overlapping. We all know that people become enthusiastic in what they are doing and wish to expand their operations. To show what I mean I shall read just a sentence or two from the annual report of the director of science service for the year ended March 31, 1953, which I think is the last year for which a report is available. This is what he says:
. . . but greatly improved laboratory facilities and more highly trained staff have resulted in a much healthier balance between applied and fundamental work. The amount of scientific work completed, during the year under review, is recorded by means of the lists of published research papers, numbering 284, at the end of this report. The value of a more comprehensive and scientific approach to economic problems is becoming increasingly apparent in the amount and quality of the applied phases of the work.
During the year five new, modern and well equipped laboratories have been completed.
And so on. I have here also the report of the minister with a list of publications. I will read just two or three of the names: "Studies on the Treatment of Contaminated Combs and Honey with High Velocity Electrons". I have no doubt that the hon. member for Middlesex East will know all about that and will be making full use of it. There are other reports listed here, and I come to one with a name so long that I can only take a run at it. It is called, as far as I can pronounce it, "the nonmutagenic action of p-p'-DDT and y-hexachlorocyclohexane". I have no doubt the minister knows all about that. I am only mentioning it to ask two questions. First of all, how is the distribution of a thing like that arranged? Second, and much more important, I want to ask this question. I have already referred to the great expansion of

the minister's department, and I have said in the house before that any man worth his oats in any job seeks to expand his department. He would not be worth his oats if he did not do so. There are various scientific agencies throughout the dominion. We have the universities and various provincial organizations, and I should like to ask the minister this question. When some new scientific work has to be done-and let me repeat that I believe in this work fully-is any attempt made to take stock of the situation and to allocate the work among the various research bodies that are capable of doing it, or is there a danger that when we have this healthy and growing organization it grows just because it likes to grow and without full account taken of the various organizations which are engaged in this kind of work? I would be glad if the minister would answer that when he speaks. I would be glad to know more about the number of scientists and whether full account is taken, in a discriminating way, of the amount of assistance which can be obtained from outside the department.
I also want to raise some question with regard to the economists. If my memory serves me correctly, there are 55 economists in the department. As I pointed out, there are really 56 because the minister is an economist too. I have here a list, which I do not propose to read, of publications of the economics division, and there again I want to raise the same question. It often occurs to me that there are two ways of looking at expenditures. One way is: Will the expenditure serve a useful purpose? The second is: Can we do without it?
We undoubtedly and naturally have been going through a period of high activity, of high government income and high productivity, and I think it would be almost inevitable that the test of public expenditure which has been applied pretty definitely is: Can we make any use of it? Will it give any good result? My question is whether the need which constantly faces us of trying not to let our expenditures get away from us-and we certainly have high taxes from which many people suffer-is having any effect on the professional services maintained by the department?

The question raised by the last speaker is one which I have referred to two or three times since eleven o'clock. I have said that the answers to this question will come on the items either of science service or experimental farms. The work is being carried on in those two sections.
I did not mean to ask the minister to do it now.

I was hoping he did not expect me to. I think two of the speakers who have spoken so far today, the first one and the last one before the hon. member took the floor, raised general questions which there probably was not much opportunity to discuss on the items. But the others were questions which I think could be much better dealt with on the items and I do not think I should proceed to answer them now and make remarks with regard to something which will be discussed a little later on. I hope that the general item can be passed now and that we can get to the other items and discuss them quite fully.

I have a question to ask which deals with policy rather than administration, and I believe this is the proper place to discuss it. When the minister is replying to the question asked by the hon. member for Acadia I should also like him to indicate the procedure followed under the co-operative marketing act with respect to the agreements between the federal government and the boards as to setting the initial price, so that it may be on record.
The other matter to which I want to refer very briefly is the question of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I have had some correspondence with the minister on that subject, and as recently as the 9th of June I had a reply to one of my letters in which the minister indicated that it is not the intention of the government to introduce legislation at this session to widen or amend the act in order to make it apply to a greater area than at the present time. In that letter reference is also made to the fact that it would not be wise to do so until agreement has been reached between the federal and provincial governments regarding financing in general.
That is the particular question I should like to have cleared up. I should like to know what agreement the minister has in mind and whether any negotiations are being carried on now between the provinces and his department with respect to the act and financing in general or are contemplated in the near future. I should also like to know whether any representations have been made to his department more recently than the ones emanating from the conference of the four western ministers of agriculture roughly six weeks or two months ago where it was unanimously recommended that the provisions of the act be made applicable to all agricultural areas of the four western provinces.
I could go into detail a great deal more but I will refrain from doing so in the interests of getting the explanation from the minister
Supply-Agriculture
that much sooner. As the minister is no doubt quite aware, the situation in many parts of Manitoba, particularly in the area which I represent, is almost as serious, judging from press reports, as it was last year. Farmers of that area who suffered almost a total loss last year are facing the same situation this year on account of the flood waters. I realize that not all these difficulties can be cleared up by projects under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act but a great deal could be done. It now appears quite clear that this is not something that happens only once in twenty or twenty-five years. It has been happening with greater regularity, and in recent years it seems to be snowballing.
There are reasons for that. One reason is the greater amount of precipitation, but there are others, and I hope that the minister can indicate that at least plans are going forward and negotiations are being held or are contemplated for this year in order that something may be done at the next session of parliament to widen the provisions of the act to include a greater proportion of the three prairie provinces. We certainly appreciate the work that has been done under the agreements between the provinces, municipalities and the federal government since about 1948. They have been of a great deal of benefit but, as I have pointed out to the minister before, the weakness of these agreements lies in the fact that the weakest link is the municipality. The assistance is based on what the individual municipality can contribute as its share of the total cost of the project. Unfortunately some municipalities which have the greatest difficulties in connection with flood waters are the least able to provide any funds. As a result there is a very severe limitation on what can be done under these agreements. I hope that the minister will clear up this question in replying to the general questions asked.

I should like to emphasize again that I am sure it is not fair to other members for me to discuss this question at this stage. The two items to which there has been particular reference are P.F.R.A. and marketing, and they are both provided for in the estimates. There may be members who are not in the house at the moment, but who expect to be here when those items are considered. It would not be fair for me to start answering questions, and to discuss those items, without those members here, because we would probably have to go back over it all again. I am quite prepared to discuss them fully when we get to the item but I wish you would let us get to the item.

Supply-Agriculture
That suits me fine; I am not insisting that the minister answer these questions now, but I did indicate that these questions having to do with policy rather than administration should be asked now.
No, the item we are discussing is administration. Questions concerning policy with regard to the different items should be asked when those items are being considered.

My understanding is a little different. We are dealing with general agricultural policy under the item of administration. I recall that in previous years when we attempted to discuss that general policy under a particular item, we were told it should have been raised on the general administration item. However, I shall not quibble about it now if the minister is willing to answer later.

I wanted to add my five cents' worth to this debate on agriculture. I was greatly impressed by the speech of the hon. member for Queens this morning, when he referred to the various claims that could be proven by statistics. One of the questions that I asked, and that he failed to answer, was who was the author of that book on statistics. I believe if I asked the farmers and my constituents, nine out of ten of them would answer that the Minister of Agriculture was the author, and he would probably take that as a compliment.
You can quote all the statistics you like, but if you go back to the farmers and ask them if they are as well off as the minister would lead them to believe they are, they will vehemently deny it. Of course, I suppose there is a certain amount of logic to that. There is no other business in the country that judges its progress on a gross income basis, and no matter how much the gross value of agricultural products may be, the cost of production is the factor that decides whether or not at the end of the year you operate at a profit or a loss. Statistics have proven that the income of the farmer has gone down some 24 per cent, and his cost of production has gone up at least 3 per cent or 4 per cent. How he can be better off than he was in other years under those conditions is more than I can understand.
There are two or three things that I am going to mention that will indicate why many industries today find themselves operating on short time or with a lesser number of employees. I do not need to go out of my own county to point that out. One day last week I was in Strathroy. I understand that one of the factories there is operating only two days a week. No doubt the employees in that

small plant have a lot less money to spend; and consequently, whether it is automobiles, clothing or food on which they spend that money, they are spending less. There are some other factors that indicate just why there is not as much money being spent. The reports of the dominion bureau of statistics on carloadings indicate that they are down considerably. I do not know that I really need to go into that, because I believe the house and the minister understand the situation. The report ending March 31, 1954, showing the cumulative totals for the first quarter of the year, indicates a 10-2 per cent drop.
The principal source of the decline in the three months total loadings are: grain, down 39,000 carloads; lumber, timber and plywood, down 6,400 carloads. In so far as commodities moving in less than carload lots are concerned, the number of carloadings of these mixed item's is down 20,000 carloads from the total of a year ago for the same period. There were 173,176 cars loaded in the three-month period a year previous, and this year for the same period the loadings are down 20,700 from that figure. I believe that indicates, just as well as anything that can be used, the present situation because that is a barometer of the business of the country.
Then, another alarming feature is the fact that imports from foreign countries are up while exports are down. Every time we buy something from abroad we hire a labourer in that foreign country to produce that article. While we have unemployment here in a good many industries, we have become so tied up with our international trade relations that countries with depreciated currencies are able to produce these goods and sell them in the Canadian market much more cheaply than we can. These nations are anxious to get into the Canadian market because of its dollar values.
Another factor that has not helped us has been the fact the United States has not lived up to its commitments so far as GATT is concerned. I am not going to go into the details of that. The United States dollar policy has certainly been detrimental so far as the sale of Canadian farm products in the world export markets is concerned. Along with this dollar policy, the practice of extending credit to nations in Europe that are in need of these goods has meant those nations will buy in the United States in preference to buying in Canada. Another indication of the trend of events is the number of commercial failures in Canada. I am not going to go into that, but the percentage is up.
Last Wednesday I asked the minister a question concerning the establishment of a floor price for Ontario wheat. I am going to

read the minister's answer. I am quoting from page 6049 of Hansard for June 16, 1954, where the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing done under the wheat board in connection with that price. The price in that regard is set otherwise.
For some time now we have listened to a debate on western wheat. All of the Ontario winter wheat buyers know quite well the wheat board, as the minister said, has nothing to do with the setting of the price for Ontario wheat. I have here a clipping from the Chatham Daily News of July 21, 1950. The parliamentary assistant will remember a meeting held at that time when it looked as though the price of Ontario grown winter wheat would decline from $1.90 to $1.60. There was quite a protest meeting and some suggestions were made as to what should be done to protect the farmer from a considerable drop in price. The price drop at that time was about 30 cents a bushel. Up until recently the price of winter wheat was ranging around $1.55. On Monday of this week I was speaking to one of the grain buyers in my county and he advised me that, so far as he could ascertain at the moment, the opening price would be somewhere around $1.25. Today I again telegraphed to some of the buyers, but so far have had no reply from them. That indicates, anyway, the thinking of the grain trade.
When we are dealing with the price of wheat I just wish to point out, as some of the other members did, that while the consumer thinks the price of food is high, he very often does not realize the percentage of the food dollar that actually goes to the producer. What I am about to quote is taken from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal. Dealing with the food dollar it says:
The farmer's share of a 14-cent loaf of bread Is 2J cents or 16 cents of every dollar spent on bread.
No doubt there are many other farm products in respect of which the percentage of the consumer's dollar that goes to the producer is higher than it is in connection with bread. Supposing the price this year for eastern grown winter wheat is $1.25, the reduction in price will be about 20 per cent. Is the price of flour ground from that wheat going to drop by 20 per cent? I doubt it very much.
Consequently the class of people in the country who are to take all the squeeze will be the producers, and the consumers will not have any of the benefit. I am afraid of that; and I doubt very much whether the price of pastry, of bread, or of flour will go down by 20 per cent.
Then, I come to another subject that a good many farmers are not too happy about,
Supply-Agriculture
and that is the grading of farm products. I think most of them believe grading has done a good deal to improve the quality of the products they put on the market. Because of grading, in many cases the product goes to the purchaser in better condition, and he receives it in better quality than in years gone by.
However, the objection of many farmers is that the grading does not carry through to the ultimate consumer, although in some lines it carries through better than in others. On the other hand the farmer finds that most of the products he has to buy are not graded. Consequently he has no way of knowing whether the product he is buying is good or not, except by depending on the integrity of the companies manufacturing the product. And hon. members know as well as I do that that varies from time to time.
Many of the things the farmers buy are dumped in this country. We heard something about dumping this morning. I am quite sure many of the products would not be purchased if the country of origin were shown on the manufactured goods dumped in here. I have textiles in mind particularly. I am certain that if they were subjected to the same scrutiny and tests to which farm products are subjected, they would not grade No. 1. Some of the products that are dumped in here are certainly not first quality. That was indicated very clearly the other evening by the hon. member for Kootenay West when he pointed out that government inspectors in the Department of Transport dealing with radio interference were quite prepared to jump on the farmer, the blacksmith or the carpenter whose motor might be causing interference, but they shied away from doing anything with the Kootenay power company. And that happens right down the line.
The inspectors jump on the farmer because he is an individual and does not wish to cause trouble; but so far as the grading of their products is concerned, the big companies are not bothered. Perhaps I might mention two or three items the farmer has to purchase which might be looked into. I would refer particularly to lumber, light bulbs, shoes, work clothes, and particularly some of the feeds and minerals that are sold to farmers. I hope some changes will be made.
I turn to one item of production with which I am familiar, namely honey. I say the grading of honey is not what it should be, and recently there have been some disputes about grades. I know that from three samples taken out of one five-pound pail of honey we got three different reports from three different sources. I know also of two

Supply-Agriculture
different samples taken from a five-pound pail that were sent to the same graders, and two different answers were received back.
Furthermore, many of the farm products today are graded after the farmer has parted with them, and he has no chance in the world of disputing or questioning the grader's report. Consequently, he finds himself in a very bad bargaining position. I shall not say any more about that because I produce honey, and some persons might think that I was trying to use some influence in respect of a product in which I am particularly interested. So I will drop the subject right there.
I have made reference to an article appearing in the Chatham News. I shall not review the whole of it, but it discusses floor prices. To the great majority of Canadian farmers the administration of the floor price program promised in 1945 has been a disappointment and a dismal failure. Whether or not we agree with the principle, so far as the farmer is concerned that program has not lived up to expectations.
I have here an article from the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Grower entitled "Who Gets the Consumer's Dollar?". I am not going to take too much of the time of the committee, but I would point out that from a 20-ounce tin of tomato juice selling for 12J cents the farmer gets only 1-8 cents. So that the farmer can scarcely be blamed for the high cost of food.
Recently when the standing committee on agriculture met we had a most interesting talk from Dr. Dimmock of that department in which he dealt with soybeans. I believe the committee appreciated what he had to say, and that a good deal of useful information was gained. In previous years when there were only one or two buyers and processors of soybeans, the growers in western Ontario, particularly those in southwestern Ontario, had difficulty in getting their crop to market because, as was pointed out, they were all harvested in a very short space of time, freight cars were not available, and they had difficulty in unloading at Toronto.
I wish to point out to the committee and to farmers in general that in this past year when an independent grain company engaged in the buying of soybeans, loading them on a boat at Port Stanley, no difficulty was encountered so far as freight-car, grading or unloading facilities at Toronto were concerned. That just goes to show what can happen when there is a bit of competition in any business. It livens it up and gives to the seller a better market at a higher price. I am pretty certain in my own mind that
[Mr. White (Middlesex East) .1
the farmers in that area stood to gain anywhere from 20 cents to 30 cents a bushel because of the competition that developed at that time. That same company is expanding its facilities at the port, and is planning to export not only soybeans but corn and wheat. A lot has been said about the part that the soybean growers association took in the marketing of that crop, but a lot of credit should be given to this private grain company which developed the market overseas and are proceeding to develop it further. I should like to draw a matter to the minister's attention which I have raised on the floor of the house on previous occasions from time to time. I hope in bringing it to his attention now my persistence will not be regarded as a nuisance. I refer to the need in the northeastern part of Alberta for an experimental farm, experimental substation,

or whatever you wish to call it, but some type of project which, combined with research, experimentation and demonstration, would assist the farmers in helping to solve their farm problems.
The minister will recall that he paid a courtesy call to the Vegreville constituency over a year ago. He will remember that at that time various delegations from miles and miles around made representations to the minister with respect to the need for such a project in that area. Generally speaking, we in western Canada have to contend with the cost of production. We are situated far from the markets. We have the problem of the cost of transportation. Therefore it is imperative that the cost of production be minimized so far as the farmer is concerned if he is to remain in business.
With regard to my constituency or northeastern Alberta generally, I should like to point out to the minister, and I think he is aware of the fact, that it is an area where the people engage in very extensive mixed farming. Time and time again, year after year, farmers from that area have received recognition in international fairs for their cattle exhibits and their grain. Year after year they have received world recognition by winning the oats championship or the barley championship. Just last year a farmer not very far from Vegreville received such recognition.
As I say, that area is definitely interested in mixed farming and there is a need for this type of thing. The reason I bring this matter to the minister's attention again is that the nearest establishment of this type is at La-combe which, for most of the farmers in my area, is more than 200 miles away. The Lacombe experimental farm is doing very useful work, but for many farmers it is difficult to go that far in order to be able to see on the spot what is going on. Therefore I hope that the minister has given this matter consideration with a view to the establishment of some such project in that area. I am not saying that it has to be as big as the Lacombe enterprise. Neither, of course, would I like to see it as small as the demonstration farms. I should like to see something in between, and I am sure that such a project would receive the widest co-operation and support from the farmers of that area and that it would be a success. Has the minister given this matter any consideration?

As the hon. member has said, this question was raised last year, I think, when my estimates were being considered, and I believe the year before. The representations made to me when I was in Alberta the summer before last were to the

The question has been discussed and the discussions have led to the consideration of where the station should be. We have in mind the possibility of having to purchase land in that locality in order to get what is required. The general policy is to rent land, but on this occasion it is thought, after some investigation having been made into the matter, that it may be difficult to get suitable land with a person on it who is prepared to carry on in that way. Rumours persist, and I have heard them in many places, that there is

some thought of moving the central experimental farm from Ottawa. Has the department any such idea in mind? Is it considering changing the location of the farm by moving it farther out from the city?

No consideration has been given to the possibility of moving the farm. There are people making suggestions all the time, of course. We listen to them, but any suggestions that have been made that anything along that line should be done at an early date have always been replied to in the negative. We do not intend to do that kind of thing. Many people have taken the position that this farm, so far as agriculture is concerned, provides opportunities that no farm in any other place could. There are so many people who come to Ottawa who probably would not go out of the city ten miles to look at an experimental farm, but in this case the farm is right here. These people are told by everybody that it is one of the beauty spots of the area and they go there. If they are farmers, they get a great deal of good out of it. If they are people from urban centres throughout the country they also get a great deal of good out of it. They find there are many things they can learn that they can apply on their own home properties which are very helpful. From that point of view we think the farm is in a good place.
In addition, I find that no matter where I go, whether I am in Europe or in Washington, a great deal of attention has been paid to keeping areas in their natural state. For example, when I go to London and look out over Hyde Park, I wonder why we do not have areas like that in our cities in Canada? The experimental farm in Ottawa is the nearest approach that we could possibly have to that. Even if it becomes necessary at some time to move some of the activities a little farther away, I do not believe that farm should be closed up or eliminated by allowing people to build on the area, or doing anything else with it. I believe it should remain there just as it is now.
I might say that I agreed when the hon. member for Greenwood was speaking that we might deal with his question either under science services or under experimental farms. In answer to his question I want to say that there has been quite a lot of discussion over the years as to whether or not research work in the Department of Agriculture, either under experimental farms or under the sciences, should be carried on by this department or by the research people. Any decisions that were made about it were made before I came here. I do not wish to take any credit for having that work done as an

increased activity on the part of the Department of Agriculture, as was suggested. This decision was made before I came here.
I was on the committee of council for some years that had to do with research. I think I am still on it because of the fact that agricultural research does come into the picture. We have always taken the position that the research work which is of benefit to farmers is better conducted on the experimental farms because the farmers can go there and see the results of it. It is much better to have it done there than to have it at some centre which is controlled by the research council. It is for that reason we have conducted the research out there. We have not thought we were overlapping in doing that kind of thing. We thought it was very necessary that work be done as close to the farmers as we could get it, in order to make it possible for them to see it.
The best illustration I have of what I am trying to say is that I can still remember when I was a boy in Ontario they used to organize trips to the Guelph farm. The hon. member who sits behind you will recall that.
They still do.

The young people of the counties of Huron and Bruce used to go down to the Guelph farm for a day. They used to talk about it from the day they went down until the day they went down there the following year. The older members of the family always encouraged the younger member to go. With that idea in mind, we think it is well to have this research work carried out on the experimental farms in so far as that is possible. Then, the people can see the results of it and go back home and put some of these things into general use to help farming operations. That is the one real reason why we keep the research in the agricultural department. We do not think we are overlapping in a way that is costing the taxpayer too much for the service that is being given.

I would not disagree with one word the minister said about doing the work he has described, and which is visited by practising farmers at Guelph and other places. I take it that the pamphlet to which I referred this morning, the name of which neither the minister nor I could pronounce, referred to fundamental research. It does not seem to me the minister's answer covers that at all. I noticed his wording. He referred to research that was being done by them or by the research people in the department and I take it the "them" meant outside agencies or by the research departments of

the provincial departments of agriculture. It seems to me the minister's answer has not covered at all what I understand is correctly described as fundamental research. Just from reading the list from which I took a couple of names this morning, it seemed to me a considerable amount of that was fundamental research, and therefore my question is still unanswered. Is the fundamental research, as well as the special research for this or that problem, being done in the federal Department of Agriculture without regard at all to the possibility of there being other agencies that might do it?

Well, if the hon. member means provincial agencies or those who are operating in connection with our university staffs, that kind of thing, there is every coordination of those services. They have access to everything we do and we have access to everything they do. We work hand in hand in doing that kind of work. If we require something done for which we have not the official or the expert, and one of the universities in Canada has them, then we get in touch with those people. There is co-operation between the two groups. I do not think any overlapping will be found.
Some of these things, like mycology and so on, that have to do with diseases of plants, are dealt with in this research work that is carried on on our experimental farms to show people how to proceed in handling them as a result of the research on that problem.

The minister's last answer does come exactly on the point to which I was referring. I just want to be sure that this is the position. Can I take it not merely that the department is ready to make use of the research facilities here or there, but that when a bit of research is to be done there is really a definite procedure by which consideration will be given to whether it can be done adequately elsewhere in Canada at the moment?
