Mr. Chairman, we have 228 illustration stations across Canada, some in all the provinces. We have a number oi experimental farms, some in each province. I believe there are four in Saskatchewan and four in Alberta, and others across the country.
It has been argued on the floor of the house-and there is no use my saying it has not been considered, because before I was in the government, some years before, I sat in the gallery and listened to a discussion on the floor of the house in which members were saying that the government of that day should make those experimental farms pay.
I believe, in principle, that any member would give the same answer to that question as was given on the floor of the house at that time, namely, that if you are going to carry on experimental work you defeat the very purpose of the operation as a farm if you pay attention to trying to make it pay. You might try to keep down the cost of carrying out experiments, and that sort of thing, to the point where it would not cost too much. But to try to make it pay a profit would be most difficult.
In connection with our 228 illustration stations our procedure is this: As a rule we go on the farm of a farmer in a district who is known to be a particularly good one. Perhaps in a hundred cases out of a hundred he makes his farm pay. That is, he is known to be able to make his farm pay in the district where he lives-because he is that type of farmer. We go to his farm and rent some of his land. We ask him to do certain things on the land in order to indicate to people the results of experiments we have carried on at the experimental farm.
We have the farmer sow a certain variety of grain, perhaps, and then at a certain season, after the grain has matured, we invite all the people in to see it. Our cereals man would be there-if a cereal were involved- or, if it were livestock, our livestock man would be there. One of those men would go to the farm and invite the neighbouring farmers to come in. He would lecture them right alongside the plot, showing them how everything is done to get certain results. The farmer who has visited the plot will take back home with him the knowledge he has gained from that visit and will apply it in order to help him on his own farm, so as to make it pay.
But I am afraid that if we were to try to demonstrate that we were making a profit from the 10 acres, 20 acres or even 50 acres of which we get control, as part of a farming operation, we might have difficulty.
[Mr. Nicholson.!
I might say in this connection that I had a suggestion made to me one time in Alberta- and I shall not use any names in what I have to say. I was travelling on a train with a certain gentleman who said, "The farmers in Alberta do not like the oil development on their farms." He was one of the oil men himself, and made the suggestion that probably the oil people might be able to gain a little more favour with the farmers if they were to select some of the most successful farmers in the district and help them to demonstrate ways and means in which they had made their farming operations successful.
I must say my reply to that gentleman was that that was exactly what we were trying to do in our illustration stations. I did not know just how it would be looked upon by the farmers themselves, if the oil people were doing it, and my reply was that they would have to find that out. My own view is that the weakness in the system, even as we apply it, is that some people find it difficult to agree that the other fellow is doing a better job than they are. And to the extent that that is true, it is sometimes difficult to have your suggestions applied. Generally speaking, however, it has been pretty successful across Canada, and I do not know that we would want to change it.

Mr. Chairman, I do not suggest in any way that what is being done should be discontinued. I think that any effort to make an experimental farm pay, when research work is being undertaken, would be very difficult. But with a fairly large vote, and with an economics branch in the minister's department, I think that department could demonstrate on a half section or a quarter section basis how mixed farming might be undertaken or conducted over a five-year or ten-year period. Profits and losses could be set out carefully, so that people would know exactly what went into the operation by way of land, interest, taxes, wages and the like, so that at the end of the year there would be a balance sheet to indicate how profitable or unprofitable the operation had been.

That was done in Saskatchewan. Perhaps I could refer to it, because it does not concern either the government there now or the government of which I was a member when I was there. It was done when the Anderson coalition government held office in Saskatchewan. They selected a number of farms over Saskatchewan, one of which I remember was near Lockwood. I remember it very well, because I was teaching school there when they were homesteading. The land was of a type which, when broken up, would grow some of the finest crops for

two or three years that could be grown anywhere. But it turned out to be comparatively light ground.
The objective they had in going there and buying that farm, one which for three years had paid very well and then had run into financial difficulties, was to see if it could be operated in a way which would make it profitable. I am not sure what is being done on that farm now, but I think most people were convinced that that land could not be operated profitably. Probably it was a good thing to prove that fact. Two years ago I had occasion to visit the experimental farm at Ottawa. Looking at some of the pigs they had out there I must say I do not think I ever saw worse pigs in my life. Perhaps they were experimenting with them, but the impression I got when I left was a very poor one, and I am sure other people who visited there must have gained the same impression. I have not visited the experimental farm for a year or so, but I hope they have a better class of pigs out there now to show the people.

Of course my hon. friend understands that some years ago it was thought by some members that we should import Landrace hogs, and try them out on the farm. We did that. After they had been there for some time and it had been demonstrated there was no advantage in them over the Yorks, an attempt was made at crossing them. We got certain results by doing that. Then, too, the Chester white was brought there for similar purposes, and there has been a crossing of those. I agree the results we have had are not too good. dry land conditions, and are very much similar to those in the North Columbia valley in East Kootenay. The minister would know what I was speaking of if I referred to Kootenay West as the Garden of Eden. We have a great variety there, greater rainfall conditions, and they vary over a few miles. In recent years newcomers have come into the area, and it is the old story of history being re-lived. In addition to that, while the Summerland experimental station is a beautiful place to visit, large numbers of people cannot travel great distances through the country. It is very awkward. I understand there are 23 illustration stations in British Columbia. from the other areas about which I have been speaking. Take the prairies, for example. It is very much a matter of difference in the soil and that is the situation we face in British Columbia. Mr. Chairman, I spoke
some time ago about the desirability of discussing two important matters. I presume this would be the item under which they could best be discussed. People from coast to coast in Canada today are wondering what is going to happen to agriculture unless something is done to regulate the amount we produce.
We are spending great sums of money through the Colombo plan and the United States point four program and through other agencies in fitting other nations to produce their own foodstuffs. That is the objective at which we aim. We say that if we can just get into India, Burma, Pakistan, the African countries, and other countries all over the world and assist them in producing their own needs then we shall not have to worry about supporting them. But we have overlooked this important fact:	Once we have
them producing all their own needs, or a major portion of them, they will have little need for our production. The result will be that we will have more difficulty in finding foreign markets for our own production.
Now, I am wondering, presuming matters develop in a normal sort of way, whether the minister has a policy or is formulating a policy in accordance with which we would be able to introduce-I do not like the word "limit", and I do not like the word "regulate", because both those words connote a certain amount of telling people what they should or should not do-but some sort of modification of our production so as to take some precaution to see that we do not produce too much more than we ourselves can consume or sell abroad, and, along the same line, probably changing our wheat production or a certain amount of it to the production of oats, barley, rye and other commodities for which we might have a good market. As I read the news, we have no difficulty in disposing of our oats and barley but we are faced with disaster if things go in the right direction, or rather in the wrong direction, in respect of our wheat. If we could manage so that we could produce more oats and more barley and less wheat, probably we might be better off. I believe I have said sufficient to indicate what is in my mind, namely the matter of regulating production so as not to produce more than we can use and can sell, beyond a certain limit, at least.
Along with that question goes this one. Are we planning to save up supplies of nonperishable goods? By that I mean goods that are non-perishable within limits, of
[Mr. Mclvor.l
course. Roosevelt used to talk a good deal about an ever-normal granary. He had a good idea, I think, in times like these. Are we planning in such a way that, in case disaster were to strike us-which it could easily do, as everyone knows-we would have in store in safe places all the oats, barley, rye, flax, mustard seed and various other kinds of seed that we would normally use, all the wheat we would normally use for a considerable length of time, as well as all the honey, sugar, soya beans, corn, peas and all that sort of thing, all of which we could so easily store?
Of course I do not wish to be an alarmist any more than does any other hon. member of this committee. But we might just as well face possibilities. There are plenty of indications that the Russians have the cobalt bomb. All hon. members know that if the cobalt bomb were used there would be little production of anything for a considerable period of time after its employment. As the minister can quite readily see, what I am wondering about is whether or not he is drafting a plan-along with the provinces, of course-under which we could preserve a considerable amount of these commodities.
As the minister and hon. members of the committee know, I gave a speech on November 17 in which I proposed that we institute an arrangement by which we would establish storage facilities on the farm-storage facilities that were acceptable and approved- under which the farmers could store their excess wheat, receive payment for that wheat stored in those facilities and be paid storage on the grain in those storage facilities just as the grain would have storage paid on it if it were in an elevator.
If we would make that sort of arrangement, I am quite positive that we could store with perfect ease on our farms all the wheat we have and that we could pay for that wheat so that the farmers would be able to carry on. Then we would have no pressure for selling abroad, something which is likely to drive governments, and people too, into a sort of panic.
While we are talking about wheat, may I say that I fail to see how we could store anything of greater intrinsic value than wheat. It seems to me that a nation which had its full wheat supplies for seven or eight years stored up in safe places would be in a most fortunate position. The wheat so stored would not be on the open market at all. It would be recognized that it is bought and paid for and that it is not for sale on fire-sale terms. To illustrate the value of such a thing as that, all we have to do is to refer to the way in which our wheat board has managed

large wheat supplies with great skill and judgment in times past. We have had vast accumulations of wheat in times past, as in 1943 and 1944, and those accumulations worried us. But the wheat board just held on until, by and by, conditions arose which used all that wheat. I fail to see why we would be doing an imprudent thing if we looked upon our wheat supplies in some such way at the present time. But as the minister well knows, if we have to rely on the big elevator companies to provide the storage for that wheat, we are going to oblige the elevator companies to build far more elevator capacity than they would be able to use under ordinary circumstances, and consequently incur an overhead which would constitute a serious liability. But if the farmers were building bins on their farms, there would not be the overhead, the need for the high degree of insurance, or the obsolescence that will be noticeable in the elevators. In those and many other ways this kind of instrument would not constitute an overhead that would threaten to impair our economic position.
That is the way I see it, and no matter how carefully I examine it nor from how many angles I look at it, the whole concept looks to me to be worthy of serious consideration. If we had similar means whereby we could store all the oats, barley, rye, flax, soya beans, sugar, honey and the other things which we could store in this country, we could then in adequate measure divert our attention from the production of wheat to the production of these other commodities, could store several years' supply of those commodities and thus would be so much the more in a safe position in respect of supply.
I just wonder what the minister has been thinking along this line. Of course, he would not take any measures of this kind without careful consultation with all the provincial governments. Any move to modify crops, plantings and so forth would be made entirely with their understanding and through their agencies among the people in the provinces so that we would work this thing out without anything like dictatorship or telling people what to do. It looks to me as though we would certainly be much safer in following a line of producing a wide variety of commodities and of storing them than we would be by running a risky business such as that which we quite obviously have been running in respect of wheat.
The question will arise as to how we can pay for all this. People will say this: You see what is happening in the United States. The Americans have a vast supply of goods which it is beginning to cost them so much

to maintain that they are trying to get out from under the cost; hence they are beginning to force their way into the world markets and they will probably wreck the whole of the world's markets.
I do not wish to enter into a prolonged or detailed discussion of this matter but I would just make this point. If we go down to the United States and see what their constitution tells them they can do, we will realize immediately that if use were made of the constitutional power which is given to congress by the constitution, there would be no difficulty whatsoever. Their constitution says specifically that congress shall coin money and determine the value thereof. There have been presidents of the United States who have used that power. One of them was Abraham Lincoln. If the United States would use that power today to pay for the wheat, to pay for the storage and the storage facilities with money out of the national credit they would immediately get out from under the grievous weight of the burden of supporting their great surpluses.
Looking at it in a very general sort of way, it does seem clear that the United States, with all her tremendous industrial potential and her vast wealth, should be able to store wheat as well as Joseph did in Egypt for seven years. It would be hard to give a reasonable explanation why what the Egyptians could do in Joseph's time could not be done by the United States today, and so with Canada.
While I am on the matter, may I say that the same power to create money is in the hands of the parliament of Canada and was used under the finance acts of 1914 and 1923, as I have outlined in speeches on the floor of the house much to the annoyance of a great many of my colleagues, I know, but nevertheless probably containing the germ of a solution to a problem which to them at the present time is utterly unsolvable, using the orthodox economic system under which we now operate.
May I ask the minister if he would tell us what he has in the way of plans as regards policies for the regulation of the production of this nation and for the storing of goods for this nation in preparation for any time of grave peril.
Before I take my seat may I draw this to the attention of hon. members. They have all thought about it many times and in thinking about it they have been filled with dread and have turned away from it. Suppose an atomic war should be waged in Europe and terrible destruction of supplies resulted in Africa and other places. Think of the tremendous need there would be for the food

which we have now and can store. We could probably save the lives of millions if we could only make use of the blessings God has given us by abundant crops in the last three or four years. Now that I have said all that, the minister might talk for a while and tell us what he has in mind for modifying the production of crops, what he has done and thinks can be done, what he contemplates and what he has in mind for the storing of crops.

Mr. Chairman, I rather hesitate to say again what I have said every year, I think, since 1939. We have had a plan all the time. The trouble is that some planners do not regard it as a plan with which they can agree. When I came here nineteen years ago and took this position I was told by Britain that we could not produce enough bacon to feed Britain, that we could not produce enough dairy products and other things to supply that market, and that therefore they were going to get them somewhere else. That, in a few words, is what we were told back in 1936. The war came in 1939 and we established a plan under which we set out to prove to the British that we could produce the food and, as every member of the house knows, by 1943 we were producing 700 million pounds of bacon for Britain, 85 per cent of all they were consuming. Then they took the trouble to send a man over here to say after the war was over they had to go back to the old method of dealing.
If hon. members do not realize that the government did something about that, well, I feel sorry for them. We held a meeting in the first week of December of every year, and we are still holding it, to indicate to farmers the things that they might produce to advantage in this country. Immediately after that statement was made by the British we communicated it to that meeting in December and suggested that we were not going to be able to sell so many hogs after the war was over and we were not going to be able to sell dairy products in the same quantities.
We did not have to do any more than tell the farmers that. We did not have to tell them what to do about it. They did the job themselves, and it has been done year by year until by the time we got into the position where Britain would not take our bacon we were not worried whether or not they did. That was not just done by nobody doing anything about it. The gentleman who is sitting here at the table has been the chairman of all these meetings except the last one, and on that occasion he was sick. I should not say he was sick, but he went out and tried to do something that a man of his
fMr. Blackmore.]
age probably should not do and he was under the weather for a few days and was not able to be there. Nevertheless we held that meeting and discussed the whole question again, and the result is to be found largely in figures which I have here. I will only use two sets of them, cattle and hogs.

Did you have a plan in 1939?

Certainly, we had a plan in 1939, and because my hon. friend did not think it was a plan he did not come back after the next election. I would suggest he follow the plan this time. Those are the facts with regard to two of the most important products. We could go through the others and come to similar conclusions in regard to those. We have a plan, and the plan has been working ever since 1935 when we first came here as a government. It has developed from that up to the point where it has brought production up to where it is today, that is the production of all commodities of which we can dispose either at home or somewhere else. There are people here who say that we depended on the United States market. We do not sell any hogs or hardly any in the United States market. We sell a few cattle in the United States market, but we are not selling anything like the number we did a few years ago. We sold over 500,000 a few years ago, and last year there were 123,000 sold outside of Canada.
Now, that is the plan, and the plan is working. In so far as storage is concerned, we have been encouraging the building of cold storages across Canada. Away back at the beginning of the century, we started to subsidize the building of cold storages. When I came here in 1935, I was told we ought to stop that policy. This idea got into the minds of people because the production in Canada was not sufficient to utilize the cold storage facilities we had. We had almost been convinced we ought to stop it when the war came along. Since the war, and while the war was on, means were developed of making use of the cold storage facilities such as the world never dreamed of before in connection with frozen products. Now, instead of starting to slow up that policy, since the war we have been stepping it up. Two years ago we changed the policy from a support of 30 per

cent of the cost of cold storage spread over four years to a 33 per cent payment in full the year the plant is built. We are, therefore, getting more and more cold storage facilities right across this country.
Well, now, that is the system of storage that has been provided for our perishable products. When we come to the non-perishable, I am in complete agreement with my hon. friend when he suggests that we farmers would be better off if we had enough storage on our own farms to store all our own grain. Personally, I believe that the most expensive way of storing grain is in a company's elevator. Because I believe that, I have enough storage space on my own farm to store all my own grain. I do not put it into the elevator until I am going to sell it. It is not a matter of paying for storage in an elevator. There are many other farmers in western Canada who follow that practice. The trouble is that many of the people who talk about this problem are the people who have not any grain to sell and never did sell any. Those of us who produce grain on our farms know what we are going to do with it, and know where to store that grain and how to look after it.
For example, a short time ago somebody started to say that we ought to have a battle with the United States over oats. I believe that the last thing in the world we ought to start a battle over with anybody is oats. In this country we cannot feed livestock without oats. There are other countries where you can, but it is an entirely different thing from feeding barley and wheat. If you feed barley and wheat, you have to have about as much oats to feed as you feed of those two grains in order to keep your stock alive while you are fattening them. The best practice to follow in western Canada is a practice I learned about the third year I was in the west. I went out in 1901 to help harvest the crop in the fall of 1901. In the summer of 1904, I helped a man for whom I was working build a barn. When we got the barn all built, and it was 84 feet long, he put a bin 16 feet wide right up the whole length of the barn.
Naturally, I said to him, "What are you going to do with that"? He said, "We have a good crop of oats this year, and I am going to fill the bin full from one end to the other." He did. I was back there in 1934 to visit the people on that farm, and they told me that was the first year that the bin had ever been empty. He used it, from one end down to the middle, to feed stock, and the next year he started from the other end and worked down to the middle. He always had a year's supply of feed oats in that bin right

Supply-A griculture
down to this period during which we had crop failure. Well, that is the only way to farm in western Canada. It is the only way to feed.
When I was out west last week I saw an item in the newspaper inserted by some people. I presume some of the members in the opposition would say it was inserted by someone on instructions from this government. It was not. The item said that there is not enough oats coming into Fort William, and we want more. I got right up on the platform and said any farmer who would ship oats out of Saskatchewan now either to Fort William or anywhere else does not know what good farming is, if he is feeding any livestock. Any farmer who kept oats down to this time of year kept the oats because he believed he needed them for feed. If he shipped them out now, and what could happen to our crop between now and the time it is harvested happened, that fellow would be without oats. Without oats he cannot feed even this wheat that is piled up there and part of which could be used for feed. These are some of the facts in connection with carrying on agriculture in this country.
We hear talk about what some other country ought to do. Certainly it is necessary for us to go down to Washington from time to time to talk to them. Certainly it is necessary for them to come up here from time to time to talk to us. The United States Secretary of Agriculture came up here one year and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I met him. We were having a terrible row about our potatoes going down into the United States. When the secretary was here I said to him, "Why, you are getting many potatoes down there from Canada; we are getting many from you." He looked surprised and said, "Is that true?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Can you give me the figures?" I said, "Yes." "Well", he said, "I'll guarantee you when I take these back and give them to the senators who have been talking about it, and show them that they did not know what they were talking about, you will not hear any more about it." And we did not hear anything more about it that year.
And so I say again in connection with these matters such as oats, and wheat we can send down to the United States, as well as what they can send up here, that we have got to get together on this subject and talk about it, get them to understand our position, and get to understand their position. Then the question of storage, the means of financing, the price we are going to get for the commodity and everything else will be on a better level than if we had not discussed it with them.
I think we have had a plan which has worked out very well, and we are in a position today where we have not surpluses such as are being talked about on the other side of the house. We do have one surplus in wheat; and the reason things have come along in the way in which they have is that we believe you can store wheat to better advantage than you can store any other agricultural product. So if we have wheat in greater quantities than we need it in Canada or greater quantities than the world needs it at the present time, it is one commodity that you can put behind an inch board and pile it up as high as you like, and it will stay there in good condition for ten years or more. They tell us it stayed in the pyramids from the time they were built until now, and that you can take wheat out from there, plant it, and it will grow. If that is true, then it is one product you can bank on when you are talking about storage. And I agree with hon. members that if we can get the storage on our farms and elsewhere it will help everybody to carry on.

I think we have profited a great deal from having the minister announce on the record that he agrees we should have wheat stored on the farms. The minister knows, of course, as everybody else in the house knows, that there was just one flaw-
There is only one word in what the hon. member has said that I would not use. I would not say they "should"; I think it would be to their best advantage if they did.

There is one flaw in the illustration-and it was an excellent illustration-in that the man who was operating the farm and storing the oats evidently was not dependent upon the immediate sale of those oats to provide him with the money to finance his next year's operations. He was probably dealing in livestock and selling it as a cash crop, or probably he was producing butter or cheese or some other commodity from which he was getting money he needed to carry on.
Of course the minister knows as well as I do that the big difficulty out in the west now, particularly in my area, is that no matter how much wheat they have stored on the farm-even behind inch boards-it is tied up until they can sell enough wheat to get the money for next year's operations. If the minister can tell us what solution he has for that problem, then I can assure him that many of the farmers in my area would cheer as soon as they heard the news.
As I have said, there are a great number of farmers in my area who have plenty of

wheat to enable them to pay off all their bills and finance their operations; but some of the saddest stories I have ever read are coming to me in letters from men who have done their very best. These are right good men who have wheat they cannot sell. They cannot borrow money on it; not enough to carry through beyond just getting their grain in. One writes me that he has exhausted-

May I say at once that the reason I did not deal with that subject is that it is not under my department, at all. We have already discussed that question for two days, and come to some conclusion about it. I do not think under the rules of the house it is proper for us to discuss it under these items.

I do not propose to violate the rules. But the simple fact is that the conclusion we came to through those days of discussion was just simply pathetic; it just left the farmers, the wheat producers of Canada, right out on a limb, with the possibility of stark ruin facing them. The minister knows that, and I do not propose to enter into a discussion about it.
The reduction of 10J cents constituted practically the total profit on the production of the wheat farmers now have, which means that all their work for two years or so has been at a loss. 1 can understand the minister's reticence to enter into a debate on this matter. However, although the matter does not come under his jurisdiction, may I say it comes under the jurisdiction of the government of which he forms a part, and in which he must have a potent voice. So we will leave it there.

Earlier [ asked the minister a question with respect to the production and distribution of Selkirk wheat. I have had complaints in connection with the distribution of it. Would the minister explain how it was produced, how many applicants received some of the wheat, and whether any of it went to the United States.

As hon. members know, Selkirk wheat is a wheat which was produced in the last few years to offset the new rust which has come into being, starting down in South America and moving north, until it has now come part way across the United States, and we even had some of it last year in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. To answer the first question, the wheat was produced by taking a sample which an elderly gentleman had produced in Manitoba, a gentleman for whom we provided a gratuity this year. It was produced in one of those accidental ways in which men of that type get certain varieties of cereals. We crossed it with other plants until we got 83276-395
Supply-Agriculture
what is known as Selkirk wheat. When that was developed we took some of it down to California and increased the quantity of it by growing it in what are our winter months so that during the succeeding season we had a very considerable amount of this wheat which we otherwise would not have had. Then we brought it back to this country and distributed it among people who had been accustomed to enlarging the quantity of wheat, so many bushels to each one, and also we sowed quite a bit of it on the lands that we are putting under irrigation out in Alberta, at Bow River and elsewhere. We grew the wheat there; we grew it at the experimental farm and elsewhere until we had a considerable amount. Then we distributed it this year to persons who desired to get it and who after they were checked were found to be people who could handle a quantity. We gave them six bushels each and they are now attempting to produce wheat which they themselves can use in succeeding seasons as seed wheat.
This wheat was given only to registered or certified seed growers, is that correct?

Yes, that was what was done in practically every case. There may have been some few cases of persons who got it who had not been producing certified seed, but very few, if any. The wheat was given out, so far as possible, to the persons that the hon. member has indicated. They are now producing and they will not only supply themselves, but they will supply neighbours and others. A check will be kept on what is done with the wheat and where it goes, and it will be distributed over the west. It is hoped that there will be a considerable amount of that wheat produced next year.

Can
the minister tell us why there was a delay in the delivery? In some cases it was after the normal seeding time before some farmers received it.

There may be some cases but I really never heard that complaint at any time. I can hardly understand why that would be a complaint this year, because the great complaint out west is that the farmers did not get their crop in until about one month later than usual. Therefore I do not know how it could have done very much harm. Of course down in the section where my hon. friend is located it is just possible that they did get their crop earlier than they did in some other places, but most of them did not get it in until quite late.

24.	Administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $5,540,940.

There is a matter which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister on this item. It is a matter with which I have had some correspondence with his officials in the past, and as a result I have received some co-operation. I know that representations have been made by other organizations as well. It is true that this is a matter that affects a local area, but it is important enough to be brought up at this time. I am referring to a situation which was created in an Annapolis county. In that county some years ago, through negotiations which were entered into between farmers, the department of agriculture of the provincial government and this department, arrangements were made for Bang's disease eradication in that county. Probably a different arrangement was made from what had been made before. Perhaps it was one which the department entered into with some mental reservation, but the letter I have here from the deputy minister said that representations were made from the provincial government and they felt they should cooperate with what was a very well organized scheme. In other words, what happened was that all the individual farmers in that county were so well organized through public meetings at schoolhouses and every other organization was brought into play that we did achieve in that county what I am told is a hundred per cent eradication of Bang's disease, and that county was declared a disease-free area. I am told by the officials of the department that it was the only one in Canada that did achieve that distinction. That happened in the years 1948 and 1949.
Since then the department has decided that it was impossible or unwise to maintain this policy with respect to all of the farmers in the area, and it is being restricted, I believe, as a general principle, to farms on which there are ten or more in a herd. I can quite appreciate that in many cases that is perfectly all right, and it would sound reasonable to farmers in areas where large herds are maintained. I suppose that 60 per cent of the farmers in that county have fewer than ten head of cattle on their farms. Up until a year ago all of those people were boasting of the fact that they had a certificate such as I hold in my hand showing that they were in a Bang's disease-free area. I have a letter which I received this morning, and it is typical of what is going on throughout the country. This is a letter

addressed to a certain farmer in the county; as a matter of fact, it is addressed to Mr. Robert E. Mason, and reads:
Dear Sir:
X am in receipt of a report covering the re-test of your herd under the-
And then there is a very long word which I would have great difficulty in pronouncing. I continue:
-Brucellosis policy of this division, and it is noted that your herd proved negative.
In other words, clear. The letter goes on:
Due to the fact that your herd contained less than ten head your certificate is being forwarded to Ottawa for cancellation.
That letter is going out to everyone who has fewer than ten cattle. A year ago they decided not to carry on the tests at allowing to representations, in which possibly I had a little part to play as well as others, the department is carrying on the tests this year. They are carrying on t.b. tests and Bang's disease tests together, but this is the last time in which they are going to do that. The farmers are being told that the whole situation will have to be changed, I suspect largely because of a shortage of veterinarians. I imagine, if the facts were known, that is the reason rather than as a matter of economy; but this was an agreement. Agreements were entered into between the farmers and the department. It is true that the department did not sign, but I have a copy of one here which was signed of one of the hundreds of thousands that were signed by the farmers throughout that county.
When you think of the tremendous amount of organization that went into that drive, and you can imagine how difficult it is to organize farmers, it is too bad that a change is being made. When you can organize rural districts of this sort and get a hundred per cent co-operation, such as was received down there, and get the assurance of the government that this program is going to be carried on, it is a great disappointment when a change is made. We are now told that the program will have to be dropped in so far as herds of fewer than ten cattle are concerned. I know that technical reasons can be given for that. I know the minister will say that we have calf vaccination and that there has been such a wide degree of acceptance of this policy that probably we are going to be in pretty good shape anyway. Certainly, that county is going to be in far better shape than before this program was initiated. The fact remains, as I say, that probably 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the farmers will lose the benefit of this. They

are losing the certificates which they have valued, and they have the feeling well, after all, this is an undertaking into which we entered with the government and now it is being broken.
And that is the frank summation of it all. If I am right in the information which I received from the department's officials, this was the one area in Canada where this situation was achieved and because of the tremendous degree of co-operation which was received and the great amount of hard work that was put into it, I wonder whether the minister cannot have the situation reviewed and have this policy which was inaugurated kept on for a while longer. The farmers have gone a long way to maintain this policy but now, as I understand it, the certificates are being picked up and they are being told that this is the end of it.
I would ask the minister to have this situation reviewed and see if it cannot be kept on for another two or three years, and by that time the situation will be so clarified that the farmers will accept this statement of the change in policy as one which would be fair and reasonable. I think this should be supported after the great deal of work which went into it during the years 1948-49.

I think the best thing I can do is just to read the directive to the district veterinarians and indicate the reasons why certain things have been done. This reads:
At the conference of district veterinarians held in Ottawa from September 23 to 25, 1954, it was the opinion of all present that the conducting of annual retests on small herds was costly and time consuming.
I think perhaps the second reason is stronger than the first if the idea was to get over the initial difficulty and get the declaration made as soon as possible. It continues:
Therefore, in accordance with the agreement reached, on and after November 1, 1952, a herd must contain a minimum of 10 head of cattle to be eligible for acceptance under the policy and that this number must be maintained at each subsequent annual retest.
That reason, of course, is tied up with the first covering cost and time consuming factors. And again:
Owners whose herds at present are under the policy will be given one year from the next annual retest to meet the above requirements and must be advised by the divisional veterinarian conducting the retest who will make a notation to that effect. Herd owners who cannot comply will have their agreements and certificates cancelled. This will not apply to federal government owned herds or licensed artificial insemination units. Agreements covering jointly owned herds will be accepted.

In Nova Scotia where areas have been provincially established for brucellosis control by individual signed agreements and reactors' slaughter without compensation, the department will continue to conduct laboratory tests but will not provide federal veterinarians for collecting blood samples.
Now, I think it will be seen that the plan is not brought to an end but that federal government activity in connection with the provision of veterinarians is discontinued. I presume that has something to do with the way in which veterinarians operate in that particular province. I have some sympathy for what my hon. friend has said but since we have gone so far with it, and apparently it has worked so well, if anything can be done to see it is maintained at the present standard then it ought to be done.

I would just like to add one further word. In the first place the minister probably knows, and if he does not I would remind him that before the scheme was brought into effect one of the conditions the farmers had to accept was that they were to pay for three tests on their own by privately operating veterinary surgeons. The farmers accepted that and expended the money in good faith. It is true they got the results of these tests, but many of them would not have paid out that money for three separate inspections had they known this was to take place. But they had the three tests made and then called upon the departmental veterinary to make the fourth and final test. These farmers were therefore called upon to make a substantial investment in the scheme when they had not intended to do so, and they made that agreement in good faith with Her Majesty the Queen as represented by the right hon. gentleman sitting across the way, though I am quite sure, in view of what has taken place, it is not one with which he would wish to associate himself. I would point out too that when the minister quotes from the memo in which it was said that many of the farmers found it difficult to live up to the regulations that there is another clause of the regulations which was distributed to the farmers and which states:
8. The veterinary director general may in his discretion cancel a certificate issued under these regulations whenever he is of opinion that the holder thereof has violated any of the provisions of his agreement, the act or these regulations or has failed to comply with any directions made pursuant to these regulations.
Certainly if any of the farmers violated the agreement the certificate should be cancelled and I do not believe any of the farmers would object to that. But do not let us cancel them by saying that only a few of

Supply-Agriculture
them were able to comply with the regulations. That is evading the question to say the least. It you are going to cancel the scheme-and I trust the minister will give further consideration to this matter as he has done in the past on other matters-then I trust he will take a very careful look at some of these clauses. Before he closes the volume and says this book is lost, then I would ask him why these certificates should be cancelled simply because a man happens to have eight or nine head of cattle.
That was agreed to by all of them. I am not conversant with all the details.
That is not my information.
But they all know what the regulations were.
Not according to this.
That is what I am told.

That is the whole argument. This was entered into in good faith by all these farmers, but now we are told that because a man may have three or four head of cattle, the certificate is to be cancelled. We are told that because of the difficulty of administration a man must have 10 head of cattle. I wish to protest against this. These men are to lose this certificate in the same manner as other people might lose a licence, and they are to be sort of blacklisted. I suggest that a man who obtained this certificate in good faith should not have his certificate cancelled and I would ask the minister to give this the most careful consideration to see if there cannot be some amelioration of this situation.

I just wish to correct a statement I made earlier. I find on checking that it was our own officials who agreed to this, and the other people were not there at that time. I would say further that as my hon. friend has brought this matter to our attention we will give it every possible consideration. I have a good deal of sympathy for the question he has raised.

I think even if there was an agreement entered into certainly you could not control brucellosis by eliminating the small herds in that county. It is quite ridiculous. If there was an agreement made with that county then I say along with the hon. member who has just spoken that it should be left up to them. I understood the minister to say these small herd owners would have their certificates sent back to them when they sent samples in. I take it these samples would have to be drawn by accredited veterinaries and they would pay the cost of drawing that sample and if they
IMr. Nowlan.]
were sent in they would be tested free by the department. Just to have the samples sent in by anyone would certainly be, I think, a questionable practice.

Mr. Chairman, on item 7 I asked the minister a certain question and I was asked to wait until this item came up. My question is what progress has been made in combating Bang's disease? I have some supplementary questions. Where does that research take place, and are there any statistics available to indicate what success has been achieved? While I am on my feet I would just like to include in that the question of another disease.

Mr. Chairman, we have been carrying on research work in connection with Bang's disease over at the animal diseases research institute at Hull ever since I have been here and indeed some time before that. That is for more than twenty years. One of the members-I do not know whether he wants to say anything about it himself or not-sent me down this note:
My herd has been accredited since 1923, thirty-one years, and the stipulation at that time, 1923, was ten head including a bull.
So it has apparently been that way for a long time. It does not just apply to Nova Scotia but applies apparently quite generally. I just wanted to make that known.
That is t.b. accreditation?

No. The hon. member keeps cattle and I think he understands the difference between Bang's disease and t.b. I am sure the member who sent me down the note understands the difference between Bang's disease and t.b. I would hope that he was speaking of Bang's disease when he said this. As far as the other matter is concerned, I think I have given the answer. Experiments are carried on over at the institute at Hull.

I have a matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. In the Roosville area of British Columbia there is a disease called vibriosis ravishing the breeding stock. I understand that the method of eradicating this disease is by either disposing of the sires or by artificial insemination. In range cattle this is quite a costly undertaking, inasmuch as the cattle are not confined as they would be in the dairy industry. The farmers are therefore finding great difficulty. While the provincial government has undertaken certain steps, representations have been made to me to the effect that there should be some contribution by the federal government in the way of grants or some similar assistance. Will the minister make some comment on this matter?
What is the disease?
Vibriosis.

The health of animals division have a report on the condition which exists there. They say it is not a reportable disease and therefore not one that we have been dealing with directly. However they are keeping a check on it. If it begins to make great difficulty I presume that more attention will be paid to it. However I imagine that it will be done through representations from the provincial department. We help in every way we can in these matters having to do with disease; but the diseases that are not reportable are, in the first instance, the responsibility of the agriculture department in the province. If they call upon us for assistance they always get it.

Now that the veterinary
director general is sitting in front of the minister maybe he could tell us when the first listed herd certificate was granted in Canada.
The doctor tells me that it was back in about 1923-he has not the exact date here-when they had the first herd.

No, Mr. Chairman. There is one question I should like to ask with regard to item 24. What experimentation or research is being carried on to control range paralysis or leucosis in poultry.

We are not carrying on any particular work with regard to that matter at the present time. Most of the work that is being carried on is being carried on provincially. I presume what my hon. friend has in mind is this matter of putting turkeys up on wire and that kind of thing in order to prevent them from getting the diseases they are accustomed to get, by keeping them off the land where it is infested with it and so on.

That was not what I had in mind, Mr. Chairman. In Middlesex and in some other places some of the poultry producers have complained that this disease is becoming serious and that so far there is no known cure for it. While there may be some experiments which are being carried on at Guelph or elsewhere, there is no official word or nothing to guide the poultry raisers as to what action they should take.
We have a man named Moynihan who is studying this disease in collaboration with provincial authorities and others. Beyond that, nothing is being done here.
There is no progress to report as yet?
No.

I notice that the cost of this brucellosis vaccine is $110,000. Can the

Supply-Agriculture
minister tell us where that vaccine is purchased and how much it costs per shot? Is any of it produced in the laboratories of the departments themselves?
It is produced in the Royal Connaught laboratories in Toronto.
What is the cost per shot?
About 37 cents; in that neighbourhood.

The minister has not answered one of my three questions. I wonder whether he would be good enough to answer the first one particularly. What progress has been made in combating Bang's disease? The other matter that I am particularly interested in is whether or not there are available any statistics to indicate the progress made in combating that disease.

I remember that a few years ago we did not accept the idea that inoculation was very helpful but after the experiences which they had in the United States we decided that it was helpful. The plan that is provided now is that the provinces do the inoculating and we supply the serum that is used for that inoculation. It has been carried on right across the country and has had very beneficial results. It is a preventive rather than stopping the disease after it gets under way.

I do not like to go further
on what we were discussing a few moments ago, but the minister used a letter on accreditation from some member of the house against the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
I did not use it against him.

You used it to prove your point, and I think it is misleading because there is a difference between accredited herds and listed herds. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings was talking about brucellosis. That had nothing to do with accredited herds. A listed herd is a herd that is tested for brucellosis. I do not believe they were listing herds as far back as 1923. We had one of the first listed herds in our county and I know that was not until after 1930.
I would not say it was the first, and I would not say it was after 1930 they started, but I do not believe it goes as far back as 1923.

They were doing something about these herds in 1923, but the listed herd name was not used until some time in the thirties, I understand. There had been a great deal of work done in connection with Bang's disease before I came here twenty years ago. I remember that one of the chief subjects of discussion at that time was what 
we were going to do about cattle with Bang's disease. It was entirely new to me. That is one of the reasons I remember it so well. It was not a thing that affected us in the west very much, but the dairy farmers down here were very much worked up about it. They came here wanting the plans which had been followed up until then changed. I am not in a position to say how far back those plans went, but they certainly had been doing a great deal about it.
I appreciate the fact that much work had been done, but what I asked the minister was when they gave their first certificate for a listed herd.

Oh, I do not think any great point is going to be served by proving that it was one year or another. I just gave you the information that a member had sent to me, and he is just as good a cattle man as my hon. friend. I merely gave you the facts as he gave them to me.

Item agreed to.
25.	Compensation for animals slaughtered, including compensation for eggs destroyed from infected premises under terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, $482,550.

I understand that the condition in Ontario now is that each county can be designated an accredited area in Ontario. Are there any counties that have not been tested yet for tuberculosis and, if so, where?

They have all been covered once. Some of them have been covered twice, some of them three times and some of them more than that. As my hon. friend knows, before they are declared to be pretty well clear they have three tests.
Then it is not true to say that the entire province of Ontario is free of tuberculosis.

I would not say it is tubercular-free but it has had one test at least. That one test may show there is a certain percentage of cattle that go down under the test. Our experience has been that when we make the second test there are usually fewer, and finally you get to where you do not find any. Then it is free.

I realize that, but there is a percentage where you do not require any tests for five years. My understanding was that the reason they had arrived at that stage was that the counties had not required any tests for five years. That means we can certainly not hope to be free of tuberculosis for a number of years, but there are places where it is less than one-half of one per cent.
One-half of one per cent will accredit them for three years and two-tenths of one per cent or below will accredit them for six years. Then you have to have a test again.

Item agreed to.
26.	Livestock and poultry, $1,644,413.
The minister made the statement a moment ago that we are not sending any hogs to the United States. It is true that we are not sending any hogs
A few but not many.

-other than for breeding purposes, but the minister left the impression that we were not sending any hogs. Probably some people would think that we were not sending any pork either. I think that that is very misleading. I should like to know how much canned pork, cooked pork and processed meats have been sent to the United States in the last year and if it is not a fact that much of our best bacon is going to the United States right now?

The position in connection with hogs is that our hogs have been higher in price than they are in the United States so hogs just do not go to the United States when you can get more for them at home as hogs. It is true, however, that there are certain cuts that can be sold in the United States. The year we had the foot-and-mouth disease we had estimated that we would sell 50 million pounds of cuts in the United States, and of course when the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic came we could not sell them and we had to can them and do other things with them. But there are certain quantities going to the United States in the form of different cuts and there is a certain amount goes over as bacon but nothing like the amounts that we used to ship out of this country as bacon. Most of our bacon is consumed here. There is nothing to prevent it going to the United States if you can get as much money there for it as here. But when anyone looks at the price of hogs at Toronto and then looks at the price at Buffalo or somewhere else he will find a very good reason why they do not go there.

When I was here from 1945 to 1949, I think in each of those years I made a speech and tried to indicate to the government the serious condition existing with respect to the production and sale of fertilizer in Canada. Before I go into the matter I want to reply to the hon. member for Kootenay East who this morning took exception to what had been said by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort in a speech earlier in the session. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort pointed out that the prices of fertilizer were such that in many cases it was not economical for farmers to use it.
In substantiation of his argument he indicated that in his constituency of Humboldt-Melfort there was a petition being circulated by farmers to more or less boycott the purchase of fertilizer. In bringing that to the attention of the house the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort Was trying to indicate that the price of fertilizer was so high farmers were in many cases taking action to boycott the purchase of it.
Now, whether or not the hon. member for Kootenay East was attempting to mislead members of the house, I cannot say. Certainly if the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort used fertilizer on part of his land, he felt it was necessary. I want to say to the minister and to the house that there can be no doubt farmers are concerned about the price of fertilizer in Canada today. In this respect the minister knows quite well-I do not think it is an exaggerated statement- that every Canadian farmer was betrayed by the Liberal government when they sold the fertilizer plants which, during the war period, were owned by the Canadian government and paid for by the Canadian taxpayers. These plants were sold to private industries at fire sale prices. All this is a matter of record and it is not my intention this afternoon to make a lengthy speech on the matter, other than to indicate that contrary to the

Supply-Agriculture
wishes of organized agriculture in Canada and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture as well as the wheat pools, and in spite of the assurances given by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the fertilizer plants belonging to the Canadian people at Welland, Trail and Calgary were sold to private enterprise.
I am very concerned about this because we hear a lot these days about the government's program to conserve our natural resources. Indeed, they have set up an individual portfolio for that purpose. Coming from an agricultural area, and having been interested in this matter, I cannot see how the government could allow the situation to exist whereby the agricultural land could deteriorate because of the lack of fertilizer. I know well that more and more farmers have become accustomed to using fertilizer. They would like to use it, and in many cases are still using it even though the price has now gone up to $120 a ton for 11-48 which is sold on the prairies. At the same time I know that many farmers, because of the price of fertilizer in relation to the cost of production, are turning away from the use of it.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the government should look into this matter; that the whole production, sale and distribution of it should be investigated in an effort to provide fertilizer at more reasonable prices. I know that during the latter part of the war period this same 11-48 was sold on the prairies at $63.50 per ton off cars. Indeed, that price existed until 1945. It went up then, of course, and the government had to step in in 1947 and ask the firms producing fertilizer to put their prices back again. Now, it has gone up, without any government control, until now this fertilizer is selling around $120 a ton in the western provinces. I feel that the farmers have a right to complain about the policy of the government in not at least taking into consideration the representations made by organized agriculture to at least keep one of these industries under government control.
The minister knows full well that in the past I have quoted commitments he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce made to the effect that one of these plants would be kept by the government so we would not have a monopoly in the production of fertilizer in Canada. That is all I have to say today in this regard, Mr. Chairman. I only hope the government will take some action and that some investigation will be made concerning this important matter.
Does the inspection of canned dog foods and canned cat foods come under this item or are there any regulations governing canned dog or cat foods?

Well, I shall try to find out at the dinner hour.

I should like to ask the minister why it is that the government still supplies pails and so on free of charge to Quebec producers of maple products.

That question, of course, has been quite naturally asked during each of the last three years, I think. I have explained that this was something we started before the war, discontinued during the war and then tried to complete after the war. I have been a little bit concerned as to why it has been necessary to carry it on so long. We had notified them at one time that this would be the last payment. Some representations have been made to us to the effect that we might have to carry on for one more year in order to clean it all up.

The present position is-and it has been that way since back about 1937-that the Quebec government are replacing pails which were used to gather sap and pans and to boil down the sap and which were covered with some lead covering to prevent them from rusting. It was found that when the sap was allowed to remain in those buckets or in the pans under certain conditions it caused lead poison to enter into the sap and that poison was found in the syrup. We undertook to assist the Quebec government in getting that equipment replaced. They were to pay a third of the cost, the farmer was to pay a third of the cost and we were to pay a third of the cost. It is on that basis that we are still paying this $100,000 this year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring a certain matter to the attention of the minister. It concerns the manner in which some of the fruit and vegetable inspectors are retired. I think this matter should be looked into so there is no recurrence of the incident which I should like to relate to the minister. The incident is as follows. It concerns one Wilfred Corp who lives in the north part of my riding. He has been a fruit and vegetable inspector for nearly 24 years, or since 1930. I understand that he never had a day's sickness and that he carried out the job very well. I have seen the man. He appears to be about 50 or 55 years of age; much younger than he actually is.
As I understand it, under the regulations in this matter, people in this type of employment are employed until they are 65, and then at that time or before they reach the age of 65 they are allowed to make application to continue their employment. I will deal with the details of that matter in just a moment but I think it might be as well to tell the story from the beginning. I have here a number of letters to which I should like to refer. The first is a copy of a letter written by Mr. Corp to one Mr. Eardley, who is fruit and vegetable inspector at Ottawa. It reads as follows:
Tavistock, Ontario, January 5, 1954.
Mr. E. A. Eardley, Chief,
Fruit and Vegetable Inspection,
Department of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Eardley:
Since I am nearing retirement age and, I believe, legislation has been passed whereby the time may

be extended if so desired, X should like to know just what the procedure is in this connection, as I should like to continue in the service.
Since my health is good and, I believe, I have not lost a day due to sickness in twenty years, I feel that I can still fulfil my duties to the satisfaction of the department.
I should appreciate hearing from you in this connection. Please advise what steps I need to take if this letter is not sufficient.
Yours respectfully,
Wilfred Corp.
The next letter in this connection is dated January 7 and is from Mr. Eardley, to whom the last letter was addressed. This letter is dated Ottawa, January 7, 1954, is addressed to Mr. W. Corp, fruit and vegetable inspector, Tavistock, Ontario, and reads as follows:
Acknowledging your letter of January 5th regarding your approaching retiring age and your desire to have your employment with this department extended beyond such age, the new legislation regarding extensions beyond the age of sixty-five has not yet been definitely passed on to the different departments and we are therefore not clear as to what the new provisions are. Certainly it appears at the moment as if this matter of extensions will not be as simple as has been indicated in certain press dispatches.
Your request will be kept in mind and when we are clear as to the new provisions we will get in touch with you and you will then be able to re-submit your request, this time through supervising inspector Frank Strong and then the district office in Hamilton.
E. A. Eardley,
Chief, Fruit and Vegetable Inspection Service.

Mr. Wilfred Corp,
Tavistock, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Corp:
It has been brought to my attention that you will reach the age of 65 years on March 24, 1954, and at that time will be eligible for three months of retiring leave to be followed by superannuation as a result of over 13 years of service as a faithful and conscientious employee of this department.
The new Public Service Superannuation Act does make provision for the extension of employees beyond the age of 65 provided that they are willing to continue and are physically fit to do so, but serious consideration must be given to the problem of the development of staff to carry on the work of the department in the future. With this letter there was attached a copy of order in council P.C. 1953-1863. That is the way it is referred to, and I presume it is order in council 1863 passed in 1953. The pertinent part reads as follows:
16. (1) Notwithstanding subsection (2)-
I will read it in a moment.
__a contributor shall cease to be employed in the
public service upon attaining sixty-five years of age unless
(a) the contributor advises the deputy head of his department, in writing, not later than thirty days prior to attaining such age, that he desires to continue to be so employed:
