(b) the contributor is certified by a qualified medical practitioner, upon examination not less than thirty days prior to attaining such age, to be physically fit to continue to be so employed;
(e) the deputy head, upon receiving from the contributor the advice referred to in paragraph (a), approves, in writing, that the contributor continue to be so employed; . . .
Paragraph (d) is not relevant because it deals with people who receive over $3,000 a year. Subsection 2 says:
(2) The deputy head of the department shall, not later than six months prior to the time when the contributor reached sixty-five years of age, notify the contributor by registered mail of the provisions of this section respecting employment in the public service after the age of sixty-five.
I should like to point out at this time, as must be very evident, that the first communication Mr. Corp had informing him he was to be retired was on the 5th of March and it indicated that he was to be retired on the 23rd. In order to apply to remain in the service he would have had to advise the deputy head of the department within thirty days, which was not possible, and he would also have had to have a physical examination at least thirty days before, and since he did not know he was going to be retired, although in January he had written asking for information, he had no opportunity. More than that, it would seem to me that before the man could be retired the condition precedent which is quite clearly set out in subsection 2 would have to be observed.
It says that the deputy head of the department shall, not later than six months prior to the time when the contributor reached 65 years of age, notify the contributor by registered mail of the provisions of this section. The whole purpose of putting that in there is to give the contributor or person who is to be retired ample warning of the fact he is to^ be retired so that if he wishes to comply with the terms of subsection 1 of section 16 he will have an opportunity of doing so. The purpose is so that he will have plenty of opportunity to make up his mind whether he would like to continue. If so, he would then have a chance to make application to the head of the department and would have plenty of opportunity to get a physical examination.
In this particular case Mr. Corp, not knowing about the regulations, wrote the department in January asking what he was supposed to do. He wanted to know if a letter would be sufficient. He received a letter in a couple of days saying that the department was not quite sure, that they did not know what they were supposed to do although the order in council was certainly passed in 1953 and this correspondence took place in 1954. 
This man wrote again and nothing was heard. He waited all during the rest of January and February and then on March 5 he received a letter saying that his services were no longer required and that he would be retired on March 23.
He had no chance to do any of the things that are set out. It is my submission that the department is entirely in the wrong, that they had no right to let this man out under these conditions and have not carried out the condition precedent of giving him six months notice. I know that section 16, subsection 1 starts off with the words "notwithstanding subsection (2)" but just the same the whole sense of the two subsections taken together is that it is impossible to carry out subsection 1 without the department having previously carried out the terms of subsection 2. In this case the matter was aggravated further by the fact that the man had written to the department, had asked for but had received no information.
An hen. Member: Carried.
Oh no, it is not.
What happened to Mr. Corp's predecessor?
Was he a Liberal?

That I could not say. I do not wish to give the name. It is not exactly fair because naturally this man is not in the house. He has been given an extension, and he will be retiring shortly. The point I would like to get at is this. If the department lays down regulations as to the procedure for retiring people, why are those regulations not followed out? When they are not, it is an easy way of getting rid of people and providing somebody else with the job. I should like the minister to tell me who is now to get the job Mr. Corp held for nearly 24 years? I would hope also that the minister would make a check that this kind of thing does not continue in the future.

I rise at this time to ask the minister a question concerning the Ontario food marketing terminal. This terminal has been built after years of labour and co-operation and is a splendid example of the result of co-operation between the government and the growers and the wholesale merchants, who worked together towards a common end. The effect of this market will be to enable the fruit and vegetable growers of Ontario to put their products on display under first class conditions, and perhaps therefore obtain higher prices than they would otherwise have obtained. It will permit the movement and delivery of articles more quickly within the Toronto market, and under more favourable conditions. Will the minister tell me if he has any arrangement whereby services may be provided for those growers who may at some time wish to export directly from that market?

The marketing centre at Toronto is one which we have been talking about for a long time. We have also had under discussion a similar set-up for Montreal. I believe both of those plants were talked about before the war and considerable negotiations had taken place suggesting that the provincial governments and this government should contribute something toward the building of those plants. Nothing had been arranged before the war, and the matter was again taken up and gone ahead with after the war.
I am quite certain there has been no undertaking on behalf of this government to pay anything towards them whatever. If there is no provision for our paying anything, of
Supply-Agriculture
course, we would not have anything to say about the conditions under which the market operates. It will be a matter entirely between the city of Toronto, I suppose, the government of Ontario and the organization that is setting up the market. We would not have anything to say about that.
Mr. Pallet!: I gather then that you have no marketing agency, and do not propose to have any marketing agency set up in that market with respect to the export of fruit and vegetables? That will depend solely on the operations of the Ontario government?

We have an organization, of course, with regard to the export of fruit and vegetables from this country to the United States or any other country. It is not necessarily associated with any market set-up such as you have in Toronto.

I should like to inquire from the minister about a problem that has come to my attention just recently concerning the importation of cherries from Italy for use as maraschino cherries. As I understand it, within a reasonably short space of time the inspection has become considerably more rigid, I believe under an agreement between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Health and Welfare. The problem that I have in mind has to do with the establishment by the department of a stated tolerance of infestation. Jusi recently a shipment was returned to Italy because the infestation was found to be quite severe. I understand that about 70 per cent of these cherries that come in are entirely free of infestation, and the suspected percentage of the remainder only runs around 2 per cent or 3 per cent. In rare cases, some of them are rather badly infested.
However, the difficulty is that the exporters themselves have no rule by which to go on; there is no published or expressed rule laid down by either department, with the result that the exporters are a little loath to ship unless they know just what standards they may be required to meet. It seems to me that no great harm could come from at least laying down some sort of standard to which they would know they must adhere, rather than having shipments coming into the country all the way from Italy, being turned back and the exporter paying the freight two ways. Quite apart from the inconvenience to the exporter in this matter, of course there is the resultant inconvenience to the importer who is likely to find himself, over a period of time, without a source of supply.

S upply-A griculture
There is the inconvenience, not only in the matter of cherries but other things as well, such as olives and so on, of having shipments held up for a considerable length of time while they are being examined. Sometimes these examinations do take a considerable length of time, and freight, storage and other charges are accumulating against the importation. I should like to ask the minister if his department will seriously consider placing a reasonable tolerance on these goods so that both the exporters and importers alike will have an idea of the standards to which they must adhere.

I understand that the infection in this particular case is the result of the fact that an insect has laid its eggs in the cherry, and they produce an insect. There is no tolerance in connection with that. If the insect is an insect we do not want in this country stinging cherries, it is just about as bad to have three or four as it is to have 50 because they will increase very rapidly. The intention is to keep them out altogether.

But these cherries are in brine. Surely the insect would be dead by this time. I am not disputing that there may have been ample reason for sending back the shipment I mentioned; that was not the main point. I merely gave that illustration. I understand that one of the reasons the shipment was turned back was that it showed traces of insects having been there which were no longer there.

I understood at first that these cherries were fresh cherries, but you say they are in brine. I am informed the real reason for turning them down is that they were not fit for human consumption, the same as if there was a worm in an apple or some other fruit. For a person to get even one of them out of a lot is going to cause considerable complaint, and therefore they are not permitted in. There is no tolerance allowed in connection with the matter. I can have the hon. member's suggestion that some tolerance be allowed considered. However I assume it has been considered many times before.

No; the information I
have is that the regulations have been tightened up considerably in the last little while, and that there have been shipments let in with some traces of infestation. As I said, quite a bit of the remaining 30 per cent would probably have only 2 per cent or 3 per cent infestation. One source of information indicated that the high was 15 per cent, and another that it was 26 per cent. It is simply ridiculous to allow imports that are in that condition.
(Mrs. Fairclough.]
But where the infestation has been only 2 or 3 per cent, in the past they have been allowed in without any complaint. I cannot see why there should not be a standard set so that these exporters will know the standard to which they are required to adhere. I am also informed that this is a bad year in so far as cherries are concerned, because of the weather conditions. Possibly by another year the condition would have cleared itself up, and there would be an almost perfect crop. At the same time there would always be a certain amount. The very fact that most of the shipments which come in are about 70 per cent free indicates that it is not a great problem at any time. The great problem is that the exporters should know what they are required to produce.
I presume they understand pretty well now, or there would not be a complaint about it.
Apparently not.

The fact that they have had them sent back indicates what the amount of the tolerance is. I would rather hope that there is not much likelihood of people on this side complaining so much about getting fruit into the country which is not entirely free of that kind of thing. I know we would raise quite a bit of trouble about it in this country if we were getting in apples, cherries, or any other fruit that was affected in the same way. If we were told after, "You let other fruit in from outside similar to this" I am sure it would raise trouble. In any case I will have the matter inquired into, see what the reasons are and whether any change can be made.
The minister will find the situation is slightly different from what he imagines, I believe, if he will inquire into the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I set out before the minister a regrettable set of circumstances concerning a certain man who, I suggest, has suffered considerable injustice.
I wonder if the minister could give me some assurance that he will look into the matter and try to get to the bottom of it.

Mr. Chairman, I quite
understand the story that has been told, although I had not heard it before. These matters come along from time to time, and usually I have to sign them. Sometimes I do not, but it may be that I did sign this one. If I did not, then it was signed by someone acting for me.
Since the age limit of 65 years was put in -and that has applied all the time I have been here, and I do not know how long

before-persons have been retired at the age of 65. After all until this last year there was no special provision made. Anyone could be retired at 65, and anyone could be allowed to continue on until the age of 70. The fact that conditions were put in last year did not make it any easier for a man to be retired. In fact there were conditions put in which made it somewhat more difficult for him to be retired.
All that had to take place before was to have an official in the department recommend such a person for continuation in office, on the ground that there was no one prepared to take his place, or that he was still in good health and able to carry on. Then that matter would come to me as minister. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred no one would have written in to me about it. I would not know the individual, or anything about him at all, other than that he had reached the age limit for retirement. Sometimes it has been asked that a person's time be extended for another year. For a time we had a rule that it could not be extended more than six months at a time. Then for another length of time we had a rule that it would not be extended more than one year at a time, and it never was for more than a year.
Then the legislation came along and, as I understand it, the legislation says there must be six months notice. It so happens that it did not come into effect until January 1, and this man had been notified before that date.
No, he had not been.
I understood from what the hon. member said that the order in council was passed before that.
Perhaps I should clear that up. I realize the facts are somewhat complicated. What happened was that apparently this order in council was passed in 1953.
What was the order in council in 1953?

Setting out the regulations and the conditions precedent-in other words the procedure-with which a person who wished to remain on after the age of 65 years had to comply. There were certain things the department had to do. The department was to give notification six months in advance of the retirement age that such a person was to be retired at a certain age, and if the person wished to remain on he had to inform the department thirty days before the retirement date, and had to have a medical examination.

I understand now that the regulations were drawn up in 1953 and
Supply-Agriculture
applied when the act came into force. The act came into force on January 1. So far as this man was concerned, there was not any six months period to carry that out.
My understanding of the case is that there were several men below him who were younger and who, until someone did retire, would have no opportunity for promotion. The promotion in this case was possible because those persons were there. The officials in the department simply took the position that this man should be retired and the other men advanced to his position. I must say I cannot take very strong exception to that procedure. However, I shall look into it and see what happened in this particular case.
I looked into one case within the last three weeks concerning which someone from the other side of the house had written to me. This individual had been dropped off and the case was reconsidered. The circumstances were not just the same as the one the hon. member has brought to my attention. There were not so many other persons available, or who were in a position where they had to be held back so long as this man was kept on.
However I shall have the matter investigated, and if there is any possibility of doing something about it, I shall have it done. But there may be the possibility that there would be no opportunity to do anything.
I will talk it over with Clark Murray and keep you informed as to his opinion of the situation.

I wonder if the minister could answer the question I asked about livestock marketing. What governs the amount of the initial payment under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act? The act states up to 80 per cent of the average cost per year. What determines whether it would be 60 per cent, 70 per cent or 80 per cent?

Under the co-operative marketing act of 1939 it is provided that any organization may apply for the right to operate with the assistance of that act. The act provides that the board which is set up to handle the operations of the act may guarantee up to 80 per cent of the average price of the last three years in order that the organization may go to the bank and make arrangements for an initial payment on the product. The limit is 80 per cent; but anyone who desires to operate under that act, either by correspondence or by coming here and meeting the board, puts up a case for their particular product. The officials

Supply-Agriculture
here naturally try to keep the guarantee down to where the government is not likely to be liable for any payment.
Then the arrangement as to what the percentage is to be is made. Some percentages have been down as low as 25 per cent, and one has been up to 80 per cent. That was in respect of Ontario cheese. The board that handles cheese in Ontario has had to guarantee 80 per cent of the price of the last three years. In that case 80 per cent of the price was 24 cents. They got a guarantee at the bank from this department. They went to the bank and borrowed sufficient money to make the initial price, based on the 24 cents, to the cheese producer. Then they go ahead and sell the product and at the end of the period we must pass an order in council giving them the authority to pay out anything that they have left before they are able to pay it out, and they pay that out as an interim or a final payment. That is the basis on which it works. It is a matter of agreement between the persons who come here and ask for it and the board who handles it.

This is the only other question I want to ask. I noticed that when the minister was in Saskatchewan the press carried a statement that no support price would be allowed to the livestock marketing board. Does that mean at this time? For example, if the price fell and a support price was given to the packers, would that apply also to the marketing boards then?
No, no; I did not say-

I understand we are at item No. 34. Item No. 35 is a livestock item; item No. 34 has to do with fruits and vegetables. I would like to dispose of it.
Mr. Pallet!: I have a question on item No. 34. Can the minister say whether or not consideration has ever been given to setting up farm marketing agreements similar to those set up in Ontario under the Ontario farm marketing act with respect to fruits and vegetables sold for processing. I refer specifically to those fruits and vegetables that are taken interprovincially for processing, and therefore at times in the past they have escaped the requirement of being sold on grade. Can the minister comment on that?

Arrangements were made during the war under the contracts which

were made at that time under which we assisted in Nova Scotia in the matter of having apples canned and dried and sold as dried apples; in other words, having them processed in different ways. But that was an arrangement made under the War Measures Act during wartime, and continued in so far as that kind of assistance was given after the war. But there have not been any other arrangements of that kind at any time.
The other matter that the hon. member for Acadia asked about is in this position. I am not sure that I completely answered his question.
This comes under the next item.
Yes. My hon. friend said that I had said something when I was out in Saskatchewan.

The press carried a statement that the minister had said that there would be no support prices under livestock, and I do not know whether that meant at this time on account of the fairly high price of livestock or whether the minister meant that even though a situation developed where a support price was paid to the packers it would not be paid to the board.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Will the committee please help the chairman to keep livestock away from the fruits and honey?

The minister answered one-half of my question and not the other half. The second half was in respect to maintaining the grade of the fruits and vegetables that are transported interprovincially for canning. Are there any provisions by which the consumers can be protected in the purchase of canned goods where the raw fruit is carried from one province into another and processed there? Within certain provinces there is protection, but I wonder whether there is any protection when the fruit is taken from one province to another for canning purposes?
No, we have no regulations or grades for fruits that are to be canned; that is, we have grades of apples that are sold fresh and grades of other fruits, but not if it is to be canned.

Item agreed to.
35. Livestock and livestock products, $1,470,981.
I should like to ask whether the same formula is in operation now as the minister mentioned some three years ago: that is, the base for 1943, 1944 and 1945. Is that changed?

That still stands. I cannot guarantee that in every case we have been

exactly able to meet conditions, but that does stand. With respect to the other matter, it was not a case of saying that it could not apply on the request that was made. I met the farmers' union executive in Saskatoon when I was west, and they indicated that they wanted to set up a marketing board under the provincial act. They asked me if the government here would agree to setting a floor price under cattle and hogs. I said we already had a floor price under hogs, 23 cents. I said, so far as cattle were concerned-and I think I reported it to the House of Commons after I came back-if we set a floor price which was higher than the United States price we would have United States cattle coming over here and it would do us more harm than good. If we set one which was lower than they were able to get in the United States, we would perhaps be criticized for that. I said, I did not think it was sound to ask us to put a floor price under cattle because the floor price was now up to the price in the United States, and it is in all probability higher than anything we could put on.
Then, the next question was: Well, is there any way in which we can get any assistance under the existing law? I said: Well there is an Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act which makes it possible for you to get up to 80 per cent of the average price of the last three years, and you can operate under that. Well, now, my understanding is that the next day when they went before the open meeting of the farmers that is what they recommended. The other statement I made was with regard to the fact that they were told that this application which had been made to me could not be accepted by the government here.

On the other hand, if a situation developed where the market price fell below the support price and you started to take the surplus from the packing plants, would you also do the same thing for the marketing boards?
I do not understand.
Would you take the surplus off their hands in the same way that you would take it off the hands of the packing houses?

The provision at the present time is that we do not take anything off anyone's hands. We go on to the market and offer 23 cents at least for hogs and we have been there all the time. If anybody else will pay more than that, we do not get any hogs. Therefore we have not had any since the beginning of last year.

Would it not be different if we had a compulsory board?

No, the compulsory board would be a provincial thing and the actual request made to us was as to whether we would allow the provisions which are already there and the authority we have in connection with interprovincial trade to be transferred to some board they might set up in, say, Winnipeg, to handle stocks arriving there, and I said that every organization that had applied for that assistance had received it and I did not know any reason why they would be turned down.

Mr. Chairman, I have had repeated complaints from the canners of chicken to the effect that they are required to can their products in a can of a certain size, the regulations governing which are, I believe, laid down by the Department of Agriculture. United States competitors are allowed to put cans of an odd size on the market in competition with our own producers. One specific case is that the Canadian canner has always to conform to a seven-ounce tin, but the United States producer can compete in the same market with a five-ounce tin which the Canadian canner is not allowed to use. The United States produces a product which looks like a bargain until you read the small print and, in fact, it is not a bargain. The Canadian producers feel it is unfair that they should be subjected to a regulation which does not apply to their United States competitor. I understand the minister's department has no jurisdiction over imported products but I bring this to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will see fit to discuss it with his colleagues with a view to seeing whether the American import can be subjected to the same regulation as is applied to the Canadian product. Would the minister like to comment on that?

We established the present regulations in 1943 and I believe there were some regulations prior to that. But these regulations were established at the request of those who were concerned with that trade. The objection was raised that the cans carry small print and usually one does not read it and it is only after you get home that you find you have not got as much as you thought you had. The canners here asked that that be made impossible here and that there be a certain size of can named in the regulation. I think everyone will agree that is probably a good thing, but we have no way of telling the United States that their producers cannot ship their cans in here unless they are of a certain size. We can only say

Supply-Agriculture
that we think our products are such that you know what you are getting when you buy them, and hope that our people will buy them in preference to the United States product. Our department certainly cannot stop it although I can discuss it with my colleagues. Even then I do not know whether we can stop it.

There is no objection to the particular size of the can. It is just that the United States producers can come in with a slightly smaller can and complete with our own producers. Two things might be suggested. One, that there might be an agreement made with the United States government requiring their producers to put their products for export in a certain size of can, or two, the department could make the regulations which apply to our producers the same as those which are applied in the United States with regard to the size of the can.

Mr. Chairman, I feel certain this is the item on which I wish to ask a few questions. The first is, how much pork was canned according to the specifications of the agricultural prices support board during 1952, and also in 1953? Second, how much was sold? Third, how much is still held? Fourth, what is the loan or pork subsidy, or whatever you like to call it, up to date? Before the minister replies I would also like to ask a few questions regarding beef. How much beef was processed, and how much was purchased and held alive? How much was sold, and how much is still on hand? Finally, what was the loss on that deal?
If the hon. member will wait a moment I will give him the exact figures. Perhaps in the meantime we could pass on to another item.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to follow up the matter raised by the hon. member for Acadia in connection with the livestock marketing board. I wonder if the minister could tell us whether the organizations in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, or any of the other provinces, have negotiated with the board in any way in an attempt to arrive at an initial price which could be guaranteed by the board and whether the negotiations have reached the stage where the price was actually discussed?

I do not think they have got to that stage as yet. As the hon. member knows, the board has to be set up under the provincial act and they have not accomplished that up to now. So far as I know there have been discussions in Manitoba between the farmers' union and

the Manitoba government and in Saskatchewan between the farmers' union and the Saskatchewan government, but they would not make any application to us until the board is set up.
The board must be set up first?
Yes.

Following up the remarks made by the hon. member for Queens on the matter of the importation of canned chicken, I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that the United States department of agriculture certainly requires exporters of canned goods from this country to adhere to the regulations set down by their department and I would think that we could make our own regulations apply in the same way.

When we were shipping canned pork into the United States we had to conform to the labels and markings they required and things of that kind and it was a matter of negotiation because we wanted to sell our pork there and we wanted it to go into their market at a price satisfactory to them, otherwise they would have added duty and we would have received no more for that pork. Therefore, we made that arrangement, and one part of it was that we put a certain type of label on the cans.

But, Mr. Chairman, this is not a matter of canned pork. It is a matter concerning anything shipped to the United States in cans and our exporters have to conform to their regulations in so far as the size of the can and the labels are concerned. That applies equally to fish, fowl, fruits, vegetables, and practically everything that we put in cans.

I understand they have to approve these things but we do not necessarily have to change the labels on all types of foodstuffs. Their regulations are intended to prevent their people being misled, and that is why they raised the objection.

I must say I support the representations made by the hon. member for Queens because, as some of the officials of the minister's department know, I had a good deal to do with the department before this standardization was put into effect back in 1943, if that is when the minister said it was.
I think it was 1943; yes.

It was quite a hectic job. As he said, the motive was to try to get around misrepresentation. But what is the

good of getting around misrepresentation on the part of canners and packers in this country if we are going to permit shippers in the American market to undercut our own people?
I will take up the matter with the other departments.

carry?

As to canned pork the amount is 98,294,076 pounds. It is all sold or arranged for. It has perhaps not all been shipped but it is all sold. The total received for it was $27,262,756.90. The loss was $31,911,076.48. That is the pork. I am getting the same figures for the beef. It was all bought in 1952. None of it was bought in 1953.
I did not know whether any was processed in 1953.

As to beef of all kinds-of course, this was quite a different deal, as is understood; it was largely frozen meat-the amount was 94,434,988 pounds; the amount received was $10,516,511.19. The loss there was about the same as that for pork; it was $33,408,941.15.
Thank you.

Can the minister tell us whether there was a different price for quality or grade? In other words, how much a pound did we get for canned pork as it was sold, and to what countries was it shipped? Some of it was shipped to Russia, I understand, and some probably to other countries. Can the minister give us the information with respect to that matter?

There were 60 million
pounds of it sold in Canada and approximately 4 million pounds in the United States. The remainder of it was sold in other countries.
As to the 60 million pounds sold in Canada, was that for local consumption?
Yes, that was for local consumption.
What was the total amount that went behind the iron curtain? Was it just this last 9 million pounds?

We have no direct information on that. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other day, that department issued a permit to Canada Packers to
Supply-Agriculture
ship some to Czechoslovakia, I think it was, which probably would be behind the iron curtain. But we sold the product to Canada Packers. We sold it to a number of different sources but some of it was sold to Canada Packers. The condition put on the sale was that the product had to be sold off this continent. That was done in order to meet regulations in the United States and so on and also to avoid its being distributed here at prices at which it was sold. It went to European countries largely. It was sold by local people. The amount that went to Czechoslovakia I think was sold by Canada Packers. I am not certain whether any of the others sold any there or not so I will not attempt to give any figures as to just what was sold.

Mr. Chairman, this is a point that the minister himself has now brought out in some detail. After all, this relates to arrangements made by his department. Can the committee not now have figures as to the sales to the countries beyond the iron curtain? He has mentioned Czechoslovakia. He has not mentioned the 8 million pounds sold to Russia. Can the minister give us the figures for the sales to countries beyond the iron curtain and the arrangements that were made in each case?

Yes. The Leader of the Opposition is perfectly correct. The product was handled by our prices support board in our department. But when it became a matter of its being shipped out of Canada there had to be permits from the Department of Trade and Commerce. In so far as we were concerned, there were 12 million pounds sold to Canada Cold Storage; there were 9 million pounds sold to Canada Packers and there were 13 million pounds sold to a combination of Canada Cold Storage and Canada Packers. Then there were 300,000 pounds sold to Vianda Limited of Switzerland.
Can the minister give the prices received along with the quantity?
The first sale was at 15 cents; the second was at 15| cents; the third one was at 16 cents and the fourth one was at 16-65 cents.
Where is the head office of Canada Cold Storage?
Montreal.

May I ask whether the minister knows whether Canada Cold Storage is affiliated in any way with Canada Packers? Is Canada Cold Storage Company a regular packing company operating in Canada the same as is Canada Packers or are they a selling agency only?

Supply-Agriculture
No, they are not a packing plant at all; they are a storage concern. So far as we know they are not associated with Canada Packers.

The minister has explained very simply that these transactions are carried out, of course, by the prices support board which actually bought the meat in the first place and arranged for its storage. Will the minister suggest to the committee that discussions did not take place with regard to where this meat was going before the sale took place? Before I ask that the question be answered, may I say that what I mean by that is this: Was there not discussion as to the destination of this meat before the arrangements were made for the sale of it?

We knew that the first 25 million were going to West Germany, that is, the 12 million and the 13 million, before it left our hands. We did not know where the 9 million were going. We made it a condition that it had to go off this continent, but we did not know where it would go. After they got it we could not impose any condition that they could not sell it in one place or another.

As I understand it, the figures that the minister has given are 12 million to Canada Cold Storage at 15 cents, 9 million to Canada Packers at 15| cents, 13 million to Canada Cold Storage at 16 cents and 300,000 to a Swiss firm at 16-65. Is that right?
That at 15J was what was sold to a combination of companies, Canada Cold Storage and Canada Packers. That is the 13 million pounds at 15f. The amount sold to Canada Packers alone was sold at 16-65.
Is that the 9 million?
That is the 9 million, and the 300,000 was sold at 16 cents.
Does the minister inform the house that at the time the sale of the 9 million at 16-65 was effected it was not then known that a permit was to be granted for the export of that to Russia?

The fact is that so far as the 9 million pounds are concerned Canada Packers, so far as we knew-and I think it is correct-bought it on speculation. They probably knew at what price other sales had been made and they bought it on speculation. We did not know where they were going to sell it. So far as I know they did not know, and eventually they did get an offer from Czechoslovakia, I think it was, and they got a permit from the Department of Trade and

Commerce. That was simply a permit to ship, as I understand it, to the country to which it had been sold. We had no idea where Canada Packers was going to sell it before we sold the 9 million pounds to them. We just made the condition that it must be off this continent.
Just so we will understand this clearly, what was the date of the sale of the 9 million pounds to Canada Packers?
January 25 by tender.
What was the date of the application for a permit by the Czechoslovaks in relation to the sale which went to Russia?
I have not got the exact date. I do not suppose the Minister of Trade and Commerce has either, but I am told it was either towards the end of March or in April.
But before that meat left it was known that the destination of the consignment that was being bought by the Czechoslovakian representative was in fact Russia.
When they got a permit to ship of course they got a permit to ship it to some place-Czechoslovakia.

That is all I want to know. At the time the government gave the permit for the sale of that 9 million pounds it was known that the destination of that order arranged through Czechoslovakian agents was Russia.
I do not think it was Russia, I think it was Czechoslovakia.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

36. Marketing of agricultural products, Including temporary appointments that may be required to be made notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $6,000, $100,000.

Item No. 40 has to do with the agricultural products board and then there is a board under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Would the minister say what this item for the marketing of agricultural products includes?
I wish the hon. member would look up at the microphone. I could hear him better when we did not have these machines.
What comes under item 36?

Item 36 is marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appointments that may be required to be made notwithstanding anything contained in
Supply-Agriculture
the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $6,000. Under that item we can appoint persons to do marketing for us, the expenditure not to exceed $6,000, without going to the civil service commission. That is all that means, and the item provides $100,000 to be used to assist in marketing farm products.

In what way is it used to market farm products? The Agricultural Prices Support Act administration markets farm products. Then there is the agricultural products board under item 40. What is the object of this? Do they do the same work as the agricultural prices support board?

The greater part of this amount is used for advertising farm products. We advertise, for example, that butter is better. We used to have that advertisement in every store where butter was being sold, meaning of course that it was better than some other things sold there also. We paid for that, and we have had similar advertisements in connection with other products. This is the vote which provides for that.

Can the minister say how long this provision permitting employment of salesmen for agricultural products outside of the civil service regulations has been in
effect?

It has been in effect ever since that vote has been in here. I am not sure that the amount has always been $6,000. But with an amount of $6,000, if we employed one person that amount would not provide for his employment for more than a year, and it would probably be for a part of a year.
Perhaps the minister could inform the committee as to the number of people who are now employed and paid under this grant and the longest term of service of any of them now employed.

The figures are given on page 111 of the book of estimates. It shows that casual assistance amounted to $4,800, and it was $4,800 last year; travelling expenses, $2,400, and it was $2,422 last year; telephones and telegrams, $200 last year and we estimate the same this year; publication of reports and other material, $5,000 last year and we estimate that for this year; advertising and other publicity, $35,000 each year; office stationery and supplies, $200 each year; marketing projects, $52,300 this year and $52,278 last year. Then, there is $100 for sundries.

The details on page 111 do not seem to indicate that there is anyone employed.

Supply-Agriculture
The first item is for casual assistance. It does not mention any one person, but that is the amount that was spent.
That is the total amount for salaries for the whole item. There is not a large staff maintained?
No. As a matter of fact, we might employ a person to go out and put in these ads or draft these ads for us, something of that kind.
May I ask what advertising was done? Was it to sell products the government owned or to stimulate the purchasing of various products?

It is to stimulate consumption of a product of which we might think, if it were not stimulated, we might have a surplus. For example, we put advertisements right across the country to the effect that "butter is better". We thought we had some butter to sell.
The government had butter to sell.
No, not necessarily the government. We thought if it were not sold it would pile up, and we would have a surplus of it so we tried to advertise it.
That is another benefit for the farmer.
It could be the storekeeper who had butter or the person who had it in storage, not necessarily the farmer.

The greater portion of the interest would be to sell that butter for the dairy farmer. They would be the parties to reap the benefit, not the storekeeper. No storekeeper would keep enough butter on hand to be worried about storage. These advertisements would be primarily of help to the farmer in the sale of the product. I do not believe the farmer or the public are aware of that fact.
No, the request was not made by the farmers.
No.

It was something that the people who are interested in producing butter and delivering butter discussed with the government. I believe they actually did have a certain amount put on butter in Ontario for that purpose. They took a cent a pound off the payment that they got, and then we put in an extra amount in order to make the amount greater, and the ads were put out all over the country.

I am in entire agreement with advertising these products. The fruitgrowers of California do the same thing to stimulate the purchase of their products. I am just wondering if every department in government as well as the Department of Agriculture have little caches of money hidden away with which they could carry that idea a little farther. I am glad to see the farmer get it, and particularly the dairy farmer. Does the same condition apply to almost every department of government? Do they have a $35,000 item with which they can say we can just help along Joe, and then he will vote for us for sure? If that is the case, it is a very handy sum of money.

I just want to say one thing. We have advertised a lot of things like onions, potatoes and so on. I want to assure my hon. friend that the item has never been hidden away. It has been stuck right out in front every time, and has been voted upon.

I should like to see an ad
from another department that would read, "Buy your ships and build them in Colling-wood". We hear talk about prices dropping by 30 per cent, but in our shipyards there has been a drop of about 100 per cent and that affects my home town. It is pretty near time this government did something about that.
I should like to know if the Department of Agriculture ever sold meat or butter at military camps for consumption by the armed forces at very cheap prices?

The only meat that we have sold so far as I can recall is some of the beef that we accumulated when we were fighting foot-and-mouth disease. I do not believe it was sold at lower prices. I think it was sold in competition with others. Everyone had to bid for it. When we had that meat, we put in bids and sold it.
Has the minister any idea of the price at which it was sold?
The beef, I understand, was sold at around 30 cents.

I have asked this question because I am informed that at Valcartier Camp near Quebec some surplus pork and beef is being sold now to private enterprise in the city of Quebec at about 18 cents a pound. I should like to know from where that surplus comes?
We would not know anything about that. The hon. member had better bring that up on the defence estimates and have it answered.

37. Freight assistance on western feed grains, $17,000,000.

Each year this item for freight assistance on western feed grain comes before us, and generally it is extended for another year. I hope it will be extended again. We in the east like to take advantage of that if we can. If it were not for the fact that we receive some assistance in connection with western feed grain we would not use nearly as much as we do. I have asked quite a number of questions tonight, and up until now I have not been critical of the minister. I am going to be critical at this moment because the minister represents the Dominion of Canada, and he is responsible for the policy that is formed by the government.
If the western farmer were getting what we have to pay for this grain I would not think so much about it, but he is not getting that price. We are paying too much for the grain at this end. There is a large disparity between what the western farmer gets for the grain, and what we have to pay for it. I should like the minister to tell me why there is such a difference in the price?

As I understand the question, Mr. Chairman, it is why someone pays the western farmer a certain price for his grain, and so far as we are concerned it is the wheat board-with others buying oats, barley and so on-and why it costs the farmer in the east so much more to get it? Well, I do not know that it is up to me to explain that. It is not anything over which we have control. We pay a very considerable part of the freight from Fort William to the east; and to the extent that the freight is paid it tends to put the price down, not up. When it gets into the hands of the dealer in Ontario, Quebec or the eastern provinces, or in British Columbia they do all kinds of things with it.
In the first place as a rule they grind it, and then they mix it with other kinds of feed to suit different animals at different ages. Then they put it in a very fancy bag, as a rule, with all kinds of inscriptions on the bag. We have no way of checking that, to find out what these costs are.
When I see a man with a trailer behind his car taking home five or six bags, sometimes I wonder why it does not cost him more, because there is so much cost in doing it that way. When I was in Ontario they took the feed home, and many of them still do. Some of them have trucks today and take it home by the truckload. Others took it home with a team and wagon, a real load of it. And it is very difficult to understand 83276-396
Supply-Agriculture
how the cost could be other than a high cost if you put only five or six bags on a trailer behind a car every time you want a little feed. If you run into town with a trailer and pull it out every few days, it is bound to have a high cost.

That is not the answer at all. No doubt there are those who do that, but that is not the answer. The fact of the matter is that we have to pay too much for this, and there is too great a spread. I think the Minister of Agriculture is responsible to some extent.
No, he is not. The minister of agriculture in Ontario is, but I am not.
Oh, well, now you are the minister acting for the Dominion of Canada.
I have nothing to do with the miller in Ontario. He gets the grain and it is his grain. If he is going to sell it to a farmer in Ontario I have nothing to do with it. That is provincial.
The dominion government controls this whole thing.
No, they do not.

You could have control over it if you wished to use your facilities to control it. And that is one place where you have fallen down, when you do not protect the farmer in every part of Canada. We have had ministers of agriculture from the west-
You are telling me one of two things, either that the farmer out west is getting too little for it, in which case I am not getting him enough, or that the fellow down here is paying too much for it.
That is true.
You will probably have to split it in the middle.

If the farmer in the west were getting a high price, it would not be so bad. But he is not getting the price. They are not getting any great amount of money after they have grown it out there. And when I get it in Ontario I have to pay more than I can afford to pay for it as feed, to feed it at a profit. And we would produce far more hogs and far more cattle if we could get it, perhaps more than you would want.

The minister knows that I have spoken on this subject every year since I came to the house. When I first came here it was a matter of an interim vote in the supplementary estimates. I remember two years ago I asked the parliamentary assistant-the minister was away and perhaps I took an unfair advantage-when this would become part of a permanent government

Supply-Agriculture
policy, and he intimated that perhaps it had. The fact that it is now in the main estimates indicates that it is now permanent government policy. I do wish to say I appreciate the fact that it is contained in the main estimates today, rather than have to wait six months as we have heretofore to find out whether it is to be voted or not. This is welcomed by the farmers in the east.
I can tell the minister that last July and early August I was engaged in a certain field activity, as were other hon. members in the house including, I presume, the right hon. gentleman. And more than one farmer to whom I happened to go during those hot July days said, when I asked him if he would vote for me, "Well, if you can tell me why middlings are so blinkety-blankety high I will vote for you". I said that if we were elected and Jimmy Gardiner was not I would reduce it.

After all, the minister has here a vote of $17 million, which is a lot of money. How is that money allocated? One can understand the purpose of it; but does not the minister's department supervise the allocation of it? And to that extent is there not a certain control over the trade?

We check it carefully. And I must say that if what my hon. friend said a moment ago could be proved I would have great difficulty in having this vote accepted by the government. I have not had it proven to me, nor have other members of the government had it proven to them, that somebody is getting away with some of the freight payments we have made.
But you suspect it.

And they would have to be getting away with it in order to bring about the condition described a moment ago. I do not really think it could be proven, and my reason for saying that is that these other costs are added on. It may be argued that they do not need to be added on at all and should not be there; but that is not the way we check. We have checked the question as to whether that grain left Fort William worth a certain amount of money, and when it got into the hands of the dealer it represented a certain amount there.
Now, if you begin adding all these other things-mixing, and adding fishmeal and a lot of other things-and sell it out at so much per hundred pounds it is difficult to get back to the price as between the western farmer and the farmer who bought the grain here. But if the idea that has been suggested could be proven, I am afraid no freight payments would be made.
[Mr. Nowlan.j

We are not kicking about the freight payments. You have said it is the dealer who is responsible. All right; we will find out if it is the dealer who is responsible. But if it is not the dealer, then somebody else is. And I would like to know who it is.

That is exactly what I said at Niagara Falls. The farmers were all there, and they were arguing this question for an hour-that the thing to do was to prove that the dealers were responsible, and then something could be done about it. Some of them thought they were, and kept insisting that they were. I say that if you are going to try to judge that, it can be done in the province of Ontario, by the government there, or in any other province.
Would the minister give the actual figures paid out for this freight subsidy in the last five years?
I have the figures here since we started. We have paid out a total of $208,711,753.87.
What years does that figure cover?

This complaint of the eastern farmers regarding the cost of feed to them is not something new; it has been going on for a good many years. I am wondering whether the department could not encourage some form of co-operation among those eastern farmers so they could buy their grain direct from the wheat board in carload lots, bring it into their district and distribute it themselves. I think it would cut down the cost of the feed by at least one-third.

There is nothing to prevent any group of farmers down here from getting together and buying direct from the wheat board or from any other organization such as the pools out there. That could be done. But the individuals have to take the initial action in connection with it.

The only difficulty as I have stated before on many occasions in the agriculture committee, is that your delivery date must be extended to almost three or four months when ordering from the wheat board direct or from any other branch. The only way you can get feed and get it at the

time you want it is to get it through the dealers. If there is any way in which the wheat board can guarantee a reasonable length of tune for delivery I am sure many farmers would buy direct, and many groups of farmers would buy direct, but they have not been able to get delivery of it probably for months after ordering. That is why they will not buy it.

Item agreed to.
44.	Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage. $3,899,245.
45.	Major irrigation and reclamation projects in the prairie provinces, $7,077,747.

I wish to make some remarks in regard to item 44. A few days ago we were discussing wheat and, as I mentioned at the time, that seemed for a while to develop into a private war between the members on both sides of the house from the province of Saskatchewan, although there were members from other parts of the country who had a very real and deep concern in this subject. There have been occasions when one of the most important questions arising under this present item seems to have been regarded as a private subject of dispute between members of this house coming from the province of Saskatchewan. I am referring to the question that has been before us on different occasions regarding the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project.
I wish to speak not merely as the Leader of the Opposition but as a member of this house representing an Ontario constituency. I regard this as a question of concern to every Canadian. It is important that we recognize it as a subject that is of interest to every Canadian. During the present session we have been discussing on different occasions the development of the St. Lawrence waterway and power project. On other occasions we have been discussing developments in other parts of the country, and I say to the credit of the members coming from parts of the country distant from the St. Lawrence seaway and power project that I have heard at no time any suggestion that this should not be supported because it was not something that brought an apparent immediate advantage to their own constituencies.
As Canadians in this house we have welcomed the information that came to us that the St. Lawrence waterways and power development would be proceeded with. As Canadians we have welcomed other developments that contribute to the general advancement of Canadians. I suggest that this long debated and very long discussed question of the South Saskatchewan dam will best be examined in the right perspective if we 83276-396J

remove it from any suggestion that it is only a question of direct interest to the people of Saskatchewan. I prefer to believe that this is a matter of just as direct concern to the people of the rest of Canada as is the St. Lawrence waterway. True, it is not as large a development; true, the amount expended would not be as great; the electric energy produced will be, in relative terms, comparatively small. The amount, however, would be very large for the area that would be affected and the benefits would be immense to the country in which the development would actually take place. We have before us now under item 44 the provision of $3,899,245 under the heading "Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage". Perhaps it would be correct to bring together the three items, 44, 45 and 46 which are in some measure related to each other.
Not item 46.
I recognize that it is primarily the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
If the hon. member will permit me, it is item 45 under which the South Saskatchewan river project comes, not item 44.
They are related items. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage of course is the-
It is the $7 million item that it comes under.

-item covering the operation of the rehabilitation act which is the act in relation to which certain inquiries were made. Item No. 45, "Major irrigation and reclamation projects in the prairie provinces" amounts to $7,077,747, and would be the item that would directly relate to this project. I recognize that. However, it is convenient if we may proceed on that basis to discuss the subject of these two items together, because the one item relates to the act under which certain inquiries have taken place, and the other is in regard to the allowances made with respect to these projects. I mention that because the engineers working under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act have been doing work in regard to this project which is in fact the basis on which much of the discussion has taken place. In fact, it was the information obtained by the engineers working under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which was largely the basis of the consideration given to this problem by the commission which was appointed to inquire into this subject.

I have no objection to the two of them being discussed at one time on the understanding that when we get through
