with them we shall have the two of them passed and we shall not come back to something else.

I am quite agreeable to doing it either way. I do it this way because there is a related aspect between these two items. It is under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act that much of the preliminary work has been done in regard to the project covered in item 44 that I am actually discussing-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreeable to the committee to discuss items 44 and 45 together?
Agreed.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe it would be desirable to go over as briefly as possible the history relating to this particular project. I do not intend to go back to the early discussions held long years ago, though I could do so for while I would not match my memories of Saskatchewan with those of the minister, who has lived there so many years and has grown up with the developments in the province, nevertheless my memories go back many years to the time when I first heard this project being discussed.
However to bring this up to the time when legislation was actually put on the statute books under which consideration was given to this project, I would mention that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was enacted in 1935 by the Conservative government under Mr. R. B. Bennett. I do not think this is something about which there will be any disagreement between myself and the minister. In fact, to some of the hon. members who have engaged in earlier debates may I just say that I am putting this on the record so as to remove some of the confusion in the Liberal folklore which has been built up on this subject. That act was put on the statute books primarily with the idea of retrieving certain prairie land, especially those of Saskatchewan, from the severity of the drought which had visited those areas.
The building of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river was a local dream of some new development made possible by the fact that the constant flow of the Saskatchewan river between high banks obviously invited the construction of a dam which would permit the development of power as well as irrigation. The building of a dam on the South Saskatchewan would permit the development of a great deal of power in that province and it would be of benefit to well over half a million acres in an area which today is one of the really tragic areas of Saskatchewan and of western Canada.
IMr. Gardiner.]
In that area, as the minister so well knows, there is tragic evidence of homes in which people lived and brought up their families. There are abandoned schools, abandoned churches, and there is the appearance of desolation in many parts of that area which we know perfectly well from the reports before us, and from the evidence of the experimental work which has been carried on, could be made rich productive areas with effective irrigation.
There is, in fact, some experimental development near Outlook in Saskatchewan where some of the finest crops, in a small area of course, are being grown where experimental irrigation has been carried out. As the minister well knows, there are within that area some beautiful homes and some substantial growth of trees which demonstrate beyond all question what can be done with that dry soil if irrigation is carried right through that area.
Now the purpose of this project is to obtain the power, not only for general use but to operate the pumping equipment for the irrigation system and in that way provide the power as well to irrigate an estimated 450,000 acres of land in central Saskatchewan.
This calls for the construction of a dam 205 feet high across the South Saskatchewan river near Outlook at a site at the mouth of Coteau creek. Associated with this plan of irrigation, and inseparable from it because the power is needed for the irrigation project, is the development of 150,000 horsepower from the water head that would be created by this dam. Part of this power would be used to pump water to heights from 15 to 120 feet to irrigate approximately 307,000 acres of the total area. The project also contemplates the provision of water for domestic use, which is greatly needed, in the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina.
This particular part is in an area that is generally known as the Palliser triangle. It was first explored between the years 1851 and 1860 by Captain John Palliser of the Royal Engineers. Warning of the problems ahead was given in his report in which he declared this to be an arid area unpromising for human habitation. It has since then been called the Palliser triangle because of his report.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this possibility has been considered for a considerable time. Engineers working under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act have been examining that site for years, testing the foundation, and carrying out experiments as to the way in which this dam could be constructed. They have reported that this is a practical project.

They have reported that the dam can be constructed. They were right there on the spot near Coteau creek and tests have demonstrated to the satisfaction of the engineers that the foundation is suitable and that there are no practical engineering difficulties standing in the way of the construction of this extremely important dam.
However, in this case the government was not satisfied to take the evidence of its own engineers. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that unless the minister is prepared to say that he is not satisfied with the engineers, who will be paid by the very money we are requested to provide at this time, then it would be proper for him to have accepted their recommendation in regard to the construction of this dam. Either those men were competent or they were not. If they were not then other engineers should be found to do the work. I believe they were competent. I believe the money should be provided for the continuance of their services. I believe those were men who knew best what could be done. Those are the men who have been right on the spot where this project is to be constructed. Those are the men who have examined the structure of the soil and the manner in which the material right there can be used for this particular purpose.
Instead of going ahead on the basis of the recommendation of the engineers who were operating under this department of government a royal commission was established to find out whether this should be proceeded with. But we have no evidence before us, Mr. Chairman, that this government at any time found it necessary to appoint a royal commission to find out whether they should proceed with the St. Lawrence waterway. I do not recall any separate royal commission established to find out whether they should proceed with the deepening of the Welland canal on the most recent occasion that they did so. I do not know that there is any evidence before us that other major enterprises have been subjected to a royal commission of inquiry. On the contrary, the government has said with some pride that it accepted the recommendation of the officials and engineers employed for the particular purpose. Why was it in this case that they were not prepared to accept the recommendations made by the engineers so long engaged in the study of this particular project?
Mr. Chairman, the report of that royal commission raised no question about the engineering possibility of this project. It raised a certain question about costs, however. It is significant that in their approach to this subject those who conducted this inquiry were largely dependent upon the
Supply-Agriculture
information given them by the very engineers whose recommendations we already have before us. From time to time we have asked questions as to whether the government was prepared to proceed with this project and the government has said on many occasions that it had not yet become convinced that this project was a practical possibility or that the time was right to undertake it.
Mr. Chairman, I need not put on the record again the amounts required to construct this project, according to the estimate of the engineers. They are before us; they are on record. I think those figures are just as reliable as are the figures before us with regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterway or the power project associated with it. I think they are just as reliable as are any of the other projected figures we are called upon to consider from time to time. I will say without any hesitation that the engineers who prepared the estimates in this case have had a much longer time to examine the subject and to study the figures they presented than have those who presented other figures upon which we have been called upon to pass.
I think we should also bear in mind the fact that we are not dealing alone with the construction of a dam; we are not dealing alone with the availability of 150,000 horsepower of electricity. We are dealing with the reclamation of soil which we know to be rich, productive soil if a water supply is made available, and we know that it can be made available in this case. I am not suggesting for one moment that we should disregard costs. I have not yet come to the point where I am prepared to accept the simple statement of the government "What's a million anyway?" I believe we should examine not only millions but single dollars. Nevertheless there are certain things which should be examined in this case or certain values which cannot be disregarded by any Canadian in coming to some conclusion on this subject.
It will be of immense importance to all of Canada if that heartland of southern Saskatchewan is made as productive as we know it can be made. A gesture of this kind should be welcomed-and I am sure it would be-by those from the maritime provinces who seek-and have obtained in certain cases, but not in as many as they would like -certain consideration there; by those from Quebec who have received consideration for certain projects; by those from Ontario who at this very moment are receiving the support of all members in this house for a project which will benefit Ontario but which will also benefit the whole of Canada; by

Supply-Agriculture
those from Manitoba and Alberta where they already know the great prosperity brought to the Lethbridge and Taber districts of southern Alberta by irrigation of this kind as well as by the people of British Columbia. They all should, and I am sure would, welcome a gesture of this kind as evidence of the feeling of all hon. members that the welfare and advancement of the province of Saskatchewan is a subject of common concern to every hon. member in the House of Commons as it is to every Canadian.
Let me now see why it is that there is so much difficulty in getting action. Why is it that there has been so much stalling on this matter? Why is it that so many explanations have been given as to why it has not been done? Why was a royal commission used to smother this project instead of proceeding on the recommendations of the engineers, as has been done on other occasions? Mr. Chairman, we have had many explanations but I must confess that hope must be stirring in the minds of some because we have a new statement from the Minister of Agriculture. I find that in Saskatoon on June 10 the Minister of Agriculture held out hope with regard to this project. It was a new hope; it was a new picture. Some of us had not heard this before. Speaking in Saskatoon with regard to this subject, the Minister of Agriculture is quoted in the Regina Leader-Post as saying -and I quote the words given in quotation marks in the article-as follows:
We have been doing all right at clearing obstruction out of the way. There were four when we started discussions and there is now only the one left-the question of power development costs-
Mr. Chairman, some of us will remember that Scotch song, "Last night there were four Marys; tonight there are but three". Now we have it down from four to one in this particular case; we have the four difficulties, which are not mentioned in detail, reduced to one, namely the question of power development costs. That matter is not important; I concede that; but it is a subject that has been known for a long time. Then we come to a quotation that I think requires some explanation. The minister is reported as saying-and again I give what appears in direct quotation marks in the article-as follows:
I am the advocate of the dam, but I am not the government of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, if those words have any meaning at all they mean simply this: I want the dam but the government will not agree to it; and since I am not the government of Canada, my wishes cannot be carried out. While we are discussing this subject, let us
(Mr. Drew.]
have an explanation as to whether there is a difference of opinion in the government with regard to this matter. We are not prying into the affairs of the government. I am putting before the committee the words which appear in quotation marks and which, unless he has been misquoted, represent the position of the minister:
X am the advocate of the dam, but I am not the government of Canada.
I repeat that those words mean nothing unless they mean that while the minister advocates the dam, the government does not advocate it.
This project, Mr. Chairman, is one which would provide, on the one hand, irrigation which would create a rich, productive area. This irrigation would once again bring happy homes to those farms which are now, for all practical purposes, in many cases abandoned. It would once again open these schools and bring into existence new and better schools. It would again bring into use these churches in which people have worshipped in the past. It would bring to that area a spirit and a confidence that would have an impact, not only upon that area itself but upon the rest of the province. Above all, it would stand as evidence of the belief of this House of Commons, representing all parts of Canada, that the welfare of the central part of southern Saskatchewan is a matter of common concern to all Canadians.

If my hon. friend is through quoting the article, I have only one criticism to make of what he said. He referred to it as a speech delivered in Saskatoon. It was not a speech. I was being questioned by a reporter of the Star-Phoenix.

Of course, I simply have the information that is contained in the article itself, and it begins with these words:
Agriculture minister J. G. Gardiner said Thursday night there could be no decision regarding the proposed South Saskatchewan river dam until the question of power development costs had been decided.
With respect to whether it was in the form of an interview or a speech-
I did not make any speech in Saskatoon at all.
I assume the minister is just as accurate in a press interview as in a speech.
Yes, I am not objecting to that. I just want to point out that it would not be correct to say that I made a speech there and said that. I did not want that quoted across the country.

I naturally accept that. I
simply have the report before me and I have

quoted the opening paragraph that gave me the impression that it was a speech or press interview that is given as the statement made by the minister. Of course, if it were in the form of a press interview, it would still represent a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture with respect to a subject that is now part of the general consideration before us. I do emphasize what I said before, that I am not suggesting that we should disregard costs.	The costs, however, are
not prohibitive.	The costs are relatively
small compared with those of a number of projects that have been undertaken by the government. They are comparatively small compared with the costs of projects that have been undertaken by single provinces in the development of their own resources.
I believe this is a practical project. I say so in the belief that the engineers' recommendations are made by men qualified to make such reports, and also because of such personal examination as I have been able to make on the site of the projected dam. There is this further aspect of the subject. Not only would it provide irrigation but it would also provide basic power for a larger power network in that area. We all know that if you have a fixed amount of continuous hydroelectric power at a low rate you can make that the basis of a largely extended use of electric power through a grid where the peak loads will be maintained by supplementary production by diesel engines, steam engines or other equipment.
In a case of this kind needed power would be made available to an extended area of farm land as well as municipalities during the off-peak period and the peak loads at higher cost could be supplied in the way I have suggested. In that way there would be a reasonably low over-all cost of power through an extended part of that area. This belief has been put forward on many occasions and I wish to say, not only as a member from Ontario but as the Leader of the Opposition, that we believe the time is long overdue for a definite decision that this project will proceed. We ask the government now to declare that it will proceed and we ask that it be done both in the interests of the people in that area and in the general interests of the whole of Canada which will benefit by the improvement of the economy of that part of Saskatchewan.

I should like to speak for a minute or two on this subject. I appreciate very much what the Leader of the Opposition has just said. There is one issue in Saskatchewan where there are no politics. Whether the member be a Liberal, a Conservative, a Social Crediter or a C.C.F.'er,
Supply-Agriculture
they are all in favour of the South Saskatchewan dam. I know that the Minister of Agriculture has received much criticism because he has not built the dam. As a matter of fact I do not know whether he deserves all the criticism that he has received because I know that he wants the dam. I know that he cannot sell the idea to the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and a few more of his colleagues, but I also know that there is probably no one in Saskatchewan who has pushed the South Saskatchewan dam any more than the Minister of Agriculture. I wish that we in the C.C.F. and Conservative parties could help him.
I can tell the Prime Minister that so far as the building of this dam is concerned there is no issue in Saskatchewan. We think it would be a good thing. In the 1930's we had the most fantastic drought that anyone could imagine. You could drive your car down the main street of a town and you could not see the end of the engine because of the dust that was blowing. We have got lots of moisture out there at the present time, but we are afraid that these same conditions may return.
In Texas, Wyoming and other states of the southern United States they have had drought. We believe that it may return to our province. That is why we are all very anxious that the dam should be built. I am not going to say much more, but I should like to say that this is a project which is in the national interest. We had fantastic relief costs during the depression and will have them again if the dam is not built. We know that if we are going to have some stability for agriculture we need to have the dam built. I hope that the Prime Minister will give consideration to doing something about this irrigation dam. It is not a political matter. It is something that everyone in the province wants.

I am sure that when the people of Saskatchewan read tomorrow what the Leader of the Opposition has said about the South Saskatchewan dam they will appreciate it. My mind goes back a few years when that grand old Conservative, Mr. John R. MacNicol, was sitting in the house. He probably knew more about irrigation than any man who sat in the house during the years he was here. There is no question that the people of Saskatchewan want and need the dam. They need it not only for farming but for power purposes. The power load in Saskatchewan has been mounting very rapidly and the power commission can hardly keep up with the demand. Last year 5,500 farms went on service and this year there will probably be 6,000.

I rode across that territory on horseback in 1905. At that time you could run a mowing machine over it and you would not get a load of hay. I wish that the Minister of Agriculture would take the Prime Minister through the Lethbridge country where they have irrigation on a similar type of land so that he could see what has been done there. We could not only take care of quite a few thousand more farmers but we could help to stabilize the whole economy of the country through that part of the country producing foodstuffs. They would be produced year after year. The farmers would not have to depend on rain.
I wish that the estimates of all departments would be brought down earlier. I think this is a subject which we should spend two or three days discussing. These estimates should not be introduced when everybody is sick and tired of sitting here and wanting to get home. These estimates should be brought down early enough so that we would still have a little pep left in us and could take some time to try to persuade the other members of the cabinet besides the Minister of Agriculture who, I am quite sure, wants to see the dam built. I earnestly suggest that the government bring down their estimates earlier next year so that we can have two or three days' debate on this project.
Will you let us get them through if they are brought down?

Mr. Chairman, those of us who have been living for a great number of years in the dry areas of Saskatchewan cannot refrain from offering a few remarks about the advantages of irrigation in a province such as Saskatchewan. I believe that the only way we learn is as a result of the experience of the past. It should not be necessary to go further than the experience of the 1930's to prove the advantages of water when dry conditions are prevalent in our part of the country. History has shown us that this condition recurs from time to time. I believe we should take those lessons that we have learned in the past into consideration in developing a program for the future that will eliminate those trials through which the people of Saskatchewan have had to pass as a result of the unfavourableness of natural conditions as they have existed from time to time.
At the moment we are utilizing much of the time of this House of Commons in trying to find a solution to the problem of what could be called, perhaps, overproduction. I believe some of this time should be utilized in considering what happens when there is
[Ur. Campbell.]
no production in this country. Our experiences in the 1930's certainly showed us that the greatest problem we have in this country is the problem of non-production as a result of climatic or other conditions that may prevail in this country of ours. I would much prefer to be in the position of endeavouring to provide a solution for the matter of production than to solve the trials and tribulations of a condition of non-production.
After all, it is in production that the wealth of Canada lies. There is only one source of wealth throughout this country, and that is production. We in Saskatchewan, as a result of past experience, wish to be in a position where we can contribute to the wealth of Canada through production, and thus stabilize the economy of this country through a continuity of production. In an area such as we have in Saskatchewan, this can result only through the proper utilization of water. The marriage of water with the soil is what results in production. This is the fundamental basis of irrigation projects throughout the world, and it is for that reason we are advocating consideration of this measure in the House of Commons. We think it is necessary for the general good of Canada because it will stabilize the continuity of wealth through production.
It is food that is essential to the people of this country. I believe it would be to our advantage to learn what action we can take, as a result of what has happened in the past, to safeguard the future. We are talking about rain in the west at the moment. It appears as though perhaps there is too much of it. However, over a period of years there has never been too much rain in Saskatchewan. Climates change, perhaps slowly sometimes and perhaps rapidly, but history repeats itself. The records we have from the beginning of time prove the fact that history repeats itself, and what has happened in western Canada in previous times is going to happen again. It is going to happen because we cannot change climatic conditions. It has been upon the production of Saskatchewan that much of the economic welfare of Canada has depended.
East of the Rocky mountains in Saskatchewan we have a condition that is not only peculiar to the Palliser triangle, to which reference has been made, but continues down through the length of Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico, part of Texas, Oklahoma, and new and old Mexico. These are the drier areas of the North American continent. I do not know of anything that is in existence at the present

time that is going to give us any hope that these climatic conditions will change. The time when we need consideration is the time when nature is unkind to us. At the moment perhaps we could forgo some of the plenteous production we have, but the time this country really appreciates production is during the dry periods, and we have had those periods in the history of our country.
We have listened to the reference to what has happened in Texas recently. During the past year over 19 per cent of the seeded wheat acreage in Texas had to be abandoned because of drought. In western Canada we have been endeavouring since 1930, as a result of our experience, to build up our economy so that what happened before shall not happen again. We want to be in a position so that if these conditions do recur we will be able to carry on production and provide the essentials for the economy of Canada. It is essential for us to supply this new wealth that is absolutely necessary from year to year. This question, therefore, bears some relationship to the economy of the whole of Canada.
We in the west are agreeable to contributing to the fullest extent possible to anything that will advance the general interest of Canada, be it the Canso project in the maritimes, the St. Lawrence project or any other project that will affect the future welfare of Canada. We ask the rest of the people of Canada to give consideration to that which is of advantage to us to maintain our living in western Canada and so that we can contribute to the welfare of Canada. Everyone knows that life is non-existent without water. It is necessary for the existence of people, necessary for the existence of livestock and necessary for the existence of industry. Perhaps if there is one reason why there is a lack of industry in western Canada it is because of the lack of water which is so essential thereto.
Life is non-existent without water, and neither grain, cereals nor grass can grow without water. All flesh that is in existence in the world is grass. If grass failed for one year in the world life would be non-existent, and that is why we in western Canada, after our experience of the 1930's, realize the importance of water to the economy of Canada. It involves the life and existence of the people of Canada as well as the people of the world.
Most of the other countries recognize the importance of the existence of water. I have been living in western Canada and in southwestern Saskatchewan for 35 years. In the springtime when the water rushes away from 83276-397
Supply-Agriculture
the melting snows because of the Chinooks or as a result of the natural development of spring into summer, every one of us who has lived in that country resents every drop of water that leaves that area. We resent the loss of the overflow that runs away in one direction into Hudson bay and in the other, because of the division of the land, into the gulf of Mexico. This water that is the lifeblood of existence to people flows away, and we watch it flow away with the deepest of emotions, realizing as we do that the water should be impounded and used for the development of the country and of the people of the world.
We hear a lot of talk about the underprivileged countries. We hear about the help we should give those people in a country like India, for instance. Well, Canada has one-half of one per cent of the irrigated land of the world. India has 55 million acres of land under irrigation, and we think of India as an underprivileged country. India is preparing right at this moment, in the Sutlej river project and the Bakra dam a $3 billion investment to provide irrigation so that they may provide food for their people. Five big projects are being developed in India. And in Pakistan, which was included in India before the division took place in that portion of the continent, at the present time they have 37 million acres under irrigation.
I have here a list of all the irrigation projects of all the countries of the world, including those supposedly underprivileged countries, showing that they have made developments through irrigation to the extent of the water they have available.
Many people are of the opinion no doubt that if all the water in western Canada were utilized for purposes of irrigation, all the land could be irrigated. But only one per cent of the total land area of Saskatchewan could be irrigated if all the water were utilized that flows down all the rivers in Saskatchewan in any one season. Hon. members will be interested to know that eight times as much water flows down the Ottawa river passing these houses of parliament as flows through all the rivers in southern Saskatchewan. So that will give an idea of the value of water to an area situated as is the province of Saskatchewan. We watch the flow of water down the Ottawa river and pay no particular attention to it. We see the water flowing through the St. Lawrence, and we think, "Well, that is just a means of commerce, whereby the ships can deliver the products of our country to other parts of the world." We pay no particular attention to it.
But in western Canada our rivers are the life of our people. Let us not for one moment

Supply-Agriculture
anticipate that things are going to continue at the level of production they have reached in the last few years. We would like to have it continue as such. If it were not for the irrigated land in the world civilization would cease to exist, because that irrigated land makes life among the people possible. There are over 188 million acres of irrigated land throughout the world which provides a livelihood for its people. We here in Canada have only one-half of one per cent of the total. And we are a progressive nation!
I would suggest that there is a great future for Canada, but we have much to do. We have heard much discussion about costs. There have been discussions through various channels of government, through commissions and committees, and the P.F.R.A. organization. I suggest that this investment is one that would repay the whole of Canada. I do not want to be a member of a government or a member of any organization that is going to go through the thirties again, or that would not at least in some way, shape or form endeavour to make some contribution to prevent a repetition of what we experienced during those years.
Down in southwestern Saskatchewan we do not have to explain our experiences of the past or what happened in those years. No one believes us when we tell them that there were months when we could not mail letters, that there were months when instead of waiting for box cars to take out our production or our wheat, as we do today, we were waiting for box cars that would bring relief to southwestern Saskatchewan. That is what we were waiting for from Ontario and Quebec, and other parts of Canada. We were waiting so that the people throughout Canada would recognize our terrible plight, a situation in which we had to sell our stock for as little as one cent a pound because there was not enough feed in the country to maintain more than one adult animal and two calves because that was the limit set by the government. No one in Canada could supply the feed for all that country that was suffering from drought.
Two-thirds of the people of Saskatchewan were on a relief basis. It cost the Dominion of Canada $200 million for that experience; and we want to see that that is not repeated in the future. Why should we not learn by experience? The people of Saskatchewan are right, and they are right in more ways than one. I think the Saskatchewan government is doing a service for the people of this country when it is offering to pay for the power that is inherent in or would be delivered through the building of the dam.
This would be a project different from any other in western Canada in that it would

have both power and irrigation in connection with it. I would not hesitate for one moment to say that a Saskatchewan government may build it, itself. And if it did, I think everybody in Saskatchewan would be behind it. But that would not be a fair thing to do. The dominion government has been responsible for the impounding of water throughout Canada, and the provincial government has been responsible for the utilization of water after it has been impounded. I think the least the Dominion of Canada could do would be to accede to the general situation prevailing throughout Canada, and that would be to grant its proportion of the cost of building a project that would be the very lifeblood of the people in western Canada, as history may well prove.
Irrespective of what we do, we are going to save money. We will save the millions that have been spent in western Canada for relief. And remember this, that there is a possibility; no, not a possibility, there is a definite probability of the development of half a million acres of irrigated land through this Saskatchewan river project.
Incidentally, this development would not help us in southwestern Saskatchewan, because our elevation is too high. We are at an elevation of around three thousand feet, and it is difficult to make water run uphill. But I am thinking of the drought years in the economy of Saskatchewan and in the economy of the Dominion of Canada, when those 500,000 acres could average 20 bushels to the acre when there was no rainfall. This would mean an enormous advantage to the Dominion of Canada.
So there could not be any loss. I do not know of any losses in these so-called underprivileged countries through their irrigation projects. They have suffered no loss through those projects. The laws of water flowing on land are the natural laws, as natural as man and wife. They are as natural as life itself. One might say they are as natural as death or as birth, or as anything else in this world. The two have to go together.
I do not want to be a member from Saskatchewan if we do not develop that which is right on our doorstep. The water is there. Every year it flows out of Saskatchewan. It is of very little use when it arrives back in Hudson bay, or in the ocean. Nature has to absorb it again in clouds, bring it back to earth and spread it over the land-and no one has been able to explain how this is done. But it is done through the design of God who has ordained that there shall be millions, billions, trillions of tons of water

spread over the country so that things may grow, and so that people may earn their livelihood through their labours.
Had this irrigation dam been built, what happened in the thirties would have been prevented. Prices were low, and all the rest of it, but there is no substitute for production. One cannot receive a price for anything unless he produces it. So the first essential is to produce. And one acre of irrigated land, we are told, will sustain 20 acres of dry land and make it possible for those other 20 acres to produce.
So let us consider what half a million acres of irrigated land will do in sustaining the economy of western Canada throughout dry years. It will eliminate resettlement in those years. We know that 5,574 persons had to be moved out of southwestern Saskatchewan, to be resettled elsewhere, on account of the drought. It seems to be money lost to have to resettle people when they can be sustained in their own environment and have an opportunity of making their own living. Trainloads of food were brought into western Canada, even from as far away as Quebec. The need for much of that could be eliminated.
I would suggest that one-half of the people of Saskatchewan were on relief in 1937. It was not an economic situation as much as a lack of production. There were no gardens; there was no wheat; there was no grain; there was no livestock. Nothing can exist without water, and we wish to eliminate that lack in the future. I do not think it is beyond the capacity of a young and growing country like Canada to make it possible for a portion of the population of this country to continue to contribute to the welfare of all our people. It has been proven by organizations such as P.F.R.A. that this irrigation development is possible. There may be persons who doubt that because of what has happened in the past in regard to power developments, as to whether coal or water may be the most economical method of developing power in the future, but that is part and parcel of the development of all our country. Wherever you find water, people and the necessary ingredients to develop industry there you will find it.
We in Saskatchewan have had a great lack of power. Water is the first essential. Give us the water and we shall have everything else. Therefore I would suggest to the federal government-
Ten o'clock.

-that we give all the support we possibly can to western Canada in the development, not of something that applies 83276-397J

to us as individuals so that we as individuals may prosper, although it should be the object of all of us to prosper through what we contribute to the rest of the Dominion of Canada. We have no right to accept the benefits of what others produce unless we produce ourselves. We have no right to expect to enjoy happiness if we do not contribute to happiness. I think that from the short-term and long-term point of view we can contribute to the welfare of all the people of Canada by giving more consideration to what is involved in the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam than we have in the past.
Indirectly we have been contributing to the building of that dam. There is the development of oil in Saskatchewan. During the last seven years Alberta has obtained over $270 million from the development of oil. Through their natural resources they contribute to the building up of additional natural resources. Saskatchewan government officials and members have claimed that Saskatchewan has 40 per cent of the oil of western Canada. Well if that oil is a natural resource it may perhaps contribute to the building up of other natural resources, the building of the dam.
